//The Story & The Domain

The Story & The Domain

The first four minutes of every interview: who you are, what the product does, and why you moved. Get the domain words right and the rest of the loop treats you as a senior engineer.

The line this defends

Software Engineer, MedicalMine India Private Limited — CharmHealth product entity; same codebase as prior Zoho role, now on billing applying AI to revenue-cycle workflows. Member Technical Staff, ZOHO Corporation — CharmHealth: HIPAA-compliant EHR SaaS serving 10,000+ US medical practices.

01

The 90-second intro

On your résuméCore

Not your life story. Four beats: what you own now, the scale it runs at, the hardest thing you shipped, and why you are in this room.

Think of it as

A film trailer. It does not tell the plot; it makes you want the ticket. Every second that is not intriguing is wasted.

How it actually works
  • Beat 1 — now: "I'm a backend engineer on CharmHealth, a US electronic health record platform. I own the AI layer in revenue-cycle billing."
  • Beat 2 — scale: the product serves 10,000+ US medical practices; state it as product scale, not your personal scale.
  • Beat 3 — hardest: one concrete rebuild. The Copilot latency work is the strongest because it has a before, an after, and a reason.
  • Beat 4 — why here: forward-looking, never a complaint about the current job.
  • Rehearse it to 90 seconds out loud. Written and spoken lengths are wildly different.
Trap

The 4-minute intro. Interviewers decide in the first minute whether you are senior, then spend the rest confirming it. Rambling reads as junior no matter how good the content is.

Say this

I'm a backend engineer on CharmHealth — a HIPAA-regulated EHR used by 10,000+ US practices. For the last year I've owned the AI layer in revenue-cycle billing: most recently I rebuilt our clinical copilot off OpenAI's Assistants API onto an in-house agentic runtime and took p95 response from 8–15 seconds to 2–5.

02

EHR — Electronic Health Record

On your résuméCore

The system of record for a patient's clinical life: demographics, encounters, diagnoses, prescriptions, labs, notes. CharmHealth is a cloud, multi-tenant EHR sold to US ambulatory practices.

Think of it as

A bank core-banking system, but the balance is a human body. Same demands: never lose a write, never show one customer another's data, never be down.

How it actually works
  • EHR vs EMR: an EMR is one clinic's chart; an EHR is designed to travel between providers. Vendors use them interchangeably; know the distinction exists.
  • The encounter is the central entity — one patient visit, hanging off it are notes, orders, diagnoses, and charges.
  • Ambulatory (outpatient clinics) vs inpatient (hospitals). CharmHealth is ambulatory — smaller practices, higher tenant count.
  • Writes are effectively append-only: you never hard-delete a clinical note, you amend it and keep the original for the audit trail.
They will ask

Three things. First, the audit trail: every read and write of patient data is logged, immutably, because it is legally discoverable — that changes your data model and your storage costs.

Second, you cannot delete. Corrections are amendments with the prior version retained, so every clinical entity is versioned rather than mutated.

Third, downtime is a patient-safety issue, not a revenue issue. A clinic mid-visit with no chart access cannot safely prescribe. That pushes you toward read-replica fallbacks and very conservative deploys.

Say this

CharmHealth is a multi-tenant ambulatory EHR — cloud-hosted, sold to independent US practices rather than hospital systems.

03

HIPAA

On your résuméCore

The US law governing protected health information. For an engineer it reduces to four hard constraints: encrypt it, log every access, minimise what you expose, and have a signed BAA with anyone you send it to.

Think of it as

A vault with a visitor book. It is not enough to lock the data — you must be able to prove afterwards exactly who opened it and why.

How it actually works
  • PHI (protected health information) = health data plus any of 18 identifiers — name, MRN, dates, even a full-face photo.
  • Encryption: in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest. Non-negotiable and easy to state.
  • Audit logging: every access to PHI is recorded with actor, subject, timestamp, reason. This is what makes support tooling hard.
  • Minimum necessary: a support agent gets the least data that lets them do the job — the principle behind your read-only props endpoints.
  • BAA (Business Associate Agreement): the contract you must have before PHI touches a third party. This is *why* you are on Azure OpenAI rather than the OpenAI public API.
They will ask

It decides your vendor before it decides your architecture. The model provider has to sign a BAA and contractually not train on your data or retain prompts — that is why our clinical features run on Azure OpenAI rather than the public API.

Then it changes the plumbing: no PHI in logs or traces, no PHI in prompt-caching keys you do not control, and an audit record for every generation that touched a chart. In practice we log a request ID and the prompt version, never the prompt body.

You expose the least PHI that still lets someone do their job. I applied it directly when I built read-only support endpoints: agents can see which step of a workflow failed and the shape of the payload, but the response is scoped at the API security layer so identifiers never leave the boundary.

Trap

Saying "we were HIPAA compliant" as a property of the code. HIPAA compliance is organisational — policies, training, BAAs, risk assessments. Your code contributes controls. Claim the controls, not the certificate.

Say this

HIPAA meant three concrete things in my work: a BAA-covered model provider, PHI never entering logs or prompts we did not control, and an audit record on every access path I added.

04

Multi-tenancy

On your résuméCore

One deployment serving many isolated customers. 10,000+ practices share the same code and, usually, the same database — so tenant isolation is a correctness property enforced on every query.

Think of it as

An apartment block. One building, one set of pipes, but a key that opens 4B must never open 4C — and the plumbing must survive one tenant filling their bath at 3am.

How it actually works
  • Isolation models: shared schema with a tenant_id column (cheapest, most dangerous), schema-per-tenant, or database-per-tenant (most isolated, worst ops).
  • The failure mode is a single query that forgets the tenant predicate. The fix is structural: enforce it in a base repository or with row-level security, never by developer discipline.
  • Noisy neighbour: one heavy tenant degrading everyone. Handled with per-tenant rate limits and quotas — exactly the problem behind your per-token switch on Copilot.
  • Per-tenant config (feature flags, BYOK keys, branding) is a lookup on every request, so it lives in Redis, not the database.
They will ask

You do not rely on every developer remembering. The tenant ID comes off the authenticated session, is put into a request-scoped context, and the data-access layer injects it into every query — application code cannot construct a query without it.

Below that, defence in depth: row-level security in the database so even a hand-written query is filtered, and a test suite that runs the whole integration pack as tenant A while asserting tenant B's rows are never visible.

Measure first — is it request volume, one pathological query, or data size? Then contain: a per-tenant token bucket at the gateway so their burst cannot exhaust the shared pool, and if it is sustained legitimate load, shard them onto their own cluster.

This is the same reasoning behind the per-token billing switch I added: a practice heavy enough to outcost a flat subscription fee is a noisy neighbour in economic terms, not just in load terms.

05

Revenue Cycle Management (RCM)

On your résuméCore

Everything between a patient walking in and the practice getting paid: eligibility check, coding the visit, submitting a claim, chasing the denial, posting the payment.

Think of it as

An invoice that a third party is allowed to argue with. You bill the insurer, not the customer, and the insurer can reject on a technicality months later.

How it actually works
  • The pipeline: eligibility → charge capture → coding → claim scrub → submit → clearinghouse → payer adjudication → ERA/remittance → payment posting → denial management → patient balance.
  • Denials are the money. A claim denied for a coding error is revenue the practice already earned and may never collect — so anything that reduces the denial rate is directly valuable.
  • Days in A/R and clean claim rate are the two metrics an RCM buyer cares about. Know these two even if you never touched them.
  • This is where AI earns its keep: coding suggestions, denial-reason classification, and appeal-letter drafting are all high-value, bounded, text-shaped problems.
They will ask

The tasks are text-in, structured-out, which is exactly what an LLM is good at. Reading a clinical note and proposing the diagnosis and procedure codes. Reading a denial and classifying the reason so it routes to the right worker. Drafting the appeal letter from the note plus the payer's stated reason.

The important design point is that none of it auto-submits. Every one is a suggestion a biller accepts or edits, because a wrong code is fraud exposure, not just a bad UX.

Trap

Do not claim you built claim adjudication or a clearinghouse integration if you did not. Say precisely which stage of the cycle your work touches — for you that is the AI-assist layer on billing workflows.

Say this

Revenue cycle is everything from eligibility check to payment posting. I work on the AI layer over it — the parts that read unstructured text and turn it into something a biller can act on.

06

Medical coding: CPT, ICD-10, HCPCS

Jargon

The controlled vocabularies a claim is written in. ICD-10 says what is wrong with the patient; CPT says what the provider did about it; the pair has to justify each other.

Think of it as

A restaurant bill where the dish names come from a fixed government menu. Invent a name, or order a steak for a patient who came in about a headache, and payment is refused.

How it actually works
  • ICD-10-CM — diagnosis codes, roughly 70,000 of them, alphanumeric like E11.9.
  • CPT — procedure/service codes, 5 digits, owned by the AMA. 99213 (an established-patient office visit) is the one you will hear most.
  • Medical necessity: the payer checks the CPT is justified by the ICD. Mismatch → denial. This pairing is the hard part of automated coding.
  • Modifiers — two-character suffixes that change meaning (-25, -59). A huge share of denials are modifier errors.
Trap

Suggesting an LLM should pick codes autonomously. Upcoding — billing for more than was done — is federal fraud. The only defensible design is suggest-and-confirm with the source text cited.

07

HL7 v2 & FHIR

Jargon

How health systems exchange data. HL7 v2 is the pipe-delimited legacy format still running most of US healthcare; FHIR is the modern REST + JSON replacement.

Think of it as

HL7 v2 is fax-era EDI that refuses to die. FHIR is the REST API someone finally wrote — and both are in production at the same hospital.

How it actually works
  • HL7 v2 — segments and pipes: PID|1||12345^^^MRN||DOE^JOHN. Ugly, ambiguous, and ubiquitous.
  • FHIR — resources (Patient, Observation, Encounter) over REST with JSON. US regulation now mandates FHIR APIs, which is why every EHR has one.
  • Interoperability is the buzzword for all of this; SMART on FHIR is the OAuth2 profile that lets third-party apps launch inside an EHR.
  • Only claim depth here if you touched it. Knowing the words is enough to sound native.
08

Explaining the Zoho → MedicalMine move

On your résuméCore

Same codebase, same product, more scope. The organisations separated, the CharmHealth product line consolidated under MedicalMine, and you moved with the product you already owned.

Think of it as

A studio spins a franchise out into its own label. The film crew moves with the film; nobody quit.

How it actually works
  • Lead with continuity: it is not a job change, it is the same product under a new entity.
  • Name the upside plainly — broader scope and better compensation. That is a normal, credible motive.
  • Never discuss the founders' personal circumstances. Indian tech is small; it reads as indiscretion and it is other people's private business.
  • Keep it to two sentences and move on. Length signals discomfort.
Trap

Volunteering more than asked. The interviewer is checking for a red flag, not collecting gossip. Two calm sentences close it; a five-minute explanation opens it.

Say this

The organisations separated and the CharmHealth product line consolidated under MedicalMine. I moved with the product I already owned — same codebase, broader scope, better compensation.

09

Your title is "Software Engineer"

On your résuméCore

Exactly as printed on the MedicalMine offer letter. Scope you can describe verbally; title you can only state as issued.

Think of it as

A passport. You can describe yourself however you like in conversation; the document says one thing and it will be checked.

How it actually works
  • Google runs third-party background verification against payroll records. A title mismatch is a real, common failure — not a theoretical risk.
  • You may absolutely say you operate at SDE-2 / senior scope with a promotion pending. Say it; do not print it.
  • 4+ years, never 5+. Internships during your B.Tech do not count under levelling guidelines. Four years is already at the top of the L4 band — claiming five gets you measured against L5 depth for no gain.
  • If asked directly about level: "My title is Software Engineer; my scope has been closer to SDE-2 — I own the AI layer in billing end to end."
Trap

Inflating either number to look stronger. Both are verified, both are cheap to check, and both turn a strong candidate into a withdrawn offer.

//The Copilot Latency Rebuild

The Copilot Latency Rebuild

Your single best story. It has a number, a cause, a design decision, and a risk mitigation — which is the full shape of a senior engineering answer.

The line this defends

Cut Charm Copilot latency 8-15s to 2-5s, rebuilding the backend onto an in-house agentic framework replacing OpenAI's deprecating Assistants API. Kept both runtimes flag-switchable, so rollback is a flip, not a 4-5 day hotfix.

01

Why the Assistants API was slow

On your résuméCore

It was a polling, server-managed state machine. You created a thread, added a message, started a run, then polled a status endpoint until it left queued and in_progress — every hop a network round trip you did not control.

Think of it as

Ordering at a counter where you cannot see the kitchen, so you walk up and ask "ready yet?" every second. The food was never the slow part.

How it actually works
  • Managed threads: conversation state lived on OpenAI's side, so every turn refetched it instead of you holding it in memory or Redis.
  • Polling, not streaming: the run status had to be polled, adding seconds of dead time even after the model had finished.
  • Opaque tool loop: when the run entered requires_action you submitted outputs and polled again — two more round trips per tool call, and tool calls could not be run in parallel.
  • No token streaming to the user: you got the answer only when the whole run completed, so time-to-first-token equalled time-to-last-token.
  • Owning the loop yourself removes the polling entirely, streams the first token immediately, and lets independent tool calls run concurrently.
Template
pythonBefore: managed run + polling. After: your own loop, streamed.
# BEFORE — Assistants API: state on their side, progress by polling
thread = client.beta.threads.create()
client.beta.threads.messages.create(thread.id, role="user", content=q)
run = client.beta.threads.runs.create(thread.id, assistant_id=A)

while run.status in ("queued", "in_progress"):
    time.sleep(0.5)                       # dead time, every turn
    run = client.beta.threads.runs.retrieve(thread.id, run.id)

# AFTER — own the loop: state is yours, tokens stream as they are made
messages = history.load(conversation_id)  # from Redis, ~1ms
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": q})

while True:
    stream = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS, stream=True,
    )
    calls = yield_from_stream(stream)      # first token reaches the UI here
    if not calls:
        break
    results = await gather(*[run_tool(c) for c in calls])   # parallel
    messages += tool_messages(calls, results)
They will ask

Mostly not in the model. The breakdown was polling dead-time between run-status checks, a full thread refetch per turn because conversation state lived server-side, and serialised tool calls — each one costing two extra round trips through requires_action and submit_tool_outputs.

On top of that the user saw nothing until the entire run completed, so perceived latency was worst-case by construction. Owning the loop killed the polling, moved history into Redis, let independent tool calls run concurrently, and streamed the first token straight to the UI.

Both, and I would separate them honestly. Real: removing poll intervals and parallelising tool calls cut wall-clock end-to-end time. Perceived: streaming dropped time-to-first-token to well under a second, so the feature felt instant even on the slower tail.

If I were reporting it rigorously I would give p50 and p95 for time-to-first-token and time-to-completion separately, because a single range hides which one moved.

Trap

Claiming the model got faster. It did not — you removed orchestration overhead. Being precise about *which* latency you cut is what separates a real engineer from someone quoting a dashboard.

Say this

The model was never the bottleneck. It was polling dead-time, a server-side thread refetch per turn, and serialised tool calls. I moved conversation state into Redis, owned the tool loop so independent calls run in parallel, and streamed tokens — so time-to-first-token went sub-second and end-to-end dropped to 2–5.

02

Agentic loop

On your résuméCore

A while-loop around a model that can call functions. Send messages, get back either a final answer or tool calls, execute them, append results, repeat until the model stops asking.

Think of it as

A junior analyst with a phone. You ask a question; they may call two colleagues before answering. Your job is to place the calls, hand back what was said, and know when to stop them dialling.

How it actually works
  • The loop is ~30 lines. The engineering is everything around it: max iterations so it cannot spin, timeouts per tool, retries with backoff, and a token budget so one query cannot cost a fortune.
  • Parallel tool calls are the biggest latency lever — modern models return several calls in one turn and they are usually independent.
  • Termination is the subtle bug: a model that keeps calling the same tool needs a loop-detection guard, not just an iteration cap.
  • Observability: log each iteration's tool names, latency, and token counts. Without that you cannot debug a slow agent, only guess.
Template
pythonThe whole pattern, with the guards that matter
async def run_agent(messages, tools, *, max_iters=8, budget=20_000):
    used = 0
    for i in range(max_iters):
        resp = await llm.chat(messages, tools=tools, stream=True)
        used += resp.usage.total_tokens
        if used > budget:
            raise BudgetExceeded(i, used)

        if not resp.tool_calls:
            return resp.content                 # normal exit

        # Independent calls run concurrently — the main latency win.
        results = await asyncio.gather(*[
            asyncio.wait_for(dispatch(c), timeout=5.0)
            for c in resp.tool_calls
        ], return_exceptions=True)

        messages.append(resp.as_message())
        for call, out in zip(resp.tool_calls, results):
            messages.append({
                "role": "tool",
                "tool_call_id": call.id,
                "content": serialise(out),      # errors go back as text
            })                                  # so the model can recover

    raise MaxIterations(max_iters)
They will ask

Three independent guards, because any one of them alone fails. A hard iteration cap. A cumulative token budget, which catches the expensive-but-short loop the iteration cap misses. And loop detection — hash the tool name plus arguments each turn, and if the same call repeats twice, break and return what you have.

The last one matters most in practice. Models rarely loop forever; they re-call the same failing tool with the same arguments because the error message did not tell them anything actionable.

It goes back to the model as a tool message containing the error text, not as an exception that kills the request. The model can usually recover — retry with corrected arguments, or tell the user it could not look something up.

The exception is anything non-retryable or unsafe: auth failures, permission denials, or a tool that mutates state. Those terminate the loop and surface a real error, because letting a model retry a write is how you get double-charges.

The forcing function was that the Assistants API was being deprecated, so we were rewriting regardless. Given that, the loop itself is small, and what we actually needed was control over the things frameworks abstract away: streaming, per-tool timeouts, our own tracing, and a flag boundary that let both runtimes coexist.

I would not argue against frameworks generally — for a greenfield product I would probably start with one. Here we already had the constraints, the surface was narrow, and owning it made the latency work possible.

Trap

Describing the loop and stopping. Anyone can write the loop. The interview signal is entirely in the guards — iteration caps, budgets, timeouts, loop detection, and how errors get back to the model.

03

Tool / function calling

On your résuméCore

You hand the model a JSON Schema for each function it may call. It replies with a name and arguments; your code executes it. The model never runs anything — it only asks.

Think of it as

A waiter with a fixed order pad. They can write "table 4, one steak, medium" — they cannot walk into the kitchen and cook.

How it actually works
  • The schema is the prompt. Vague descriptions produce wrong calls far more often than a weak model does. Describe when *not* to use the tool as well as when to.
  • Arguments are model-generated, therefore untrusted input. Validate against the schema, then authorise against the *user's* permissions — never the agent's.
  • Keep the tool count low. Beyond roughly 15–20 tools, selection accuracy falls off; group them or route in two stages.
  • Strict mode / constrained decoding guarantees syntactically valid JSON, which removes a whole class of parse-retry latency.
Template
pythonA tool definition, and the authorisation that must wrap it
TOOLS = [{
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "get_claim_status",
    "description": (
      "Look up the adjudication status of a submitted claim. "
      "Use only when the user names a specific claim ID. "
      "Do NOT use for questions about how claims work in general."
    ),
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "claim_id": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^CLM[0-9]{8}$"},
      },
      "required": ["claim_id"],
      "additionalProperties": False,
    },
    "strict": True,          # constrained decoding: always valid JSON
  },
}]

def dispatch(call, *, actor):
    args = validate(call.arguments, SCHEMAS[call.name])   # shape
    # Authorise as the human, never as the agent. The model chose the
    # claim_id, so it is user input with extra steps.
    if not can_read_claim(actor, args["claim_id"]):
        return {"error": "not authorised for this claim"}
    return REGISTRY[call.name](**args)
They will ask

Authorisation at dispatch, evaluated against the authenticated human's tenant and role — not against the agent. The model's output is user-controlled input, so it gets exactly the same treatment as a request parameter someone typed.

In a multi-tenant EHR that is the whole ballgame. The agent runs inside a request context that already carries the tenant; the data layer injects it, so a cross-tenant ID simply returns not-found rather than being trusted because a model produced it.

First, invest in the descriptions — most misfires are ambiguity between two tools, fixed by stating what each one is *not* for. Second, cap the count: past roughly twenty, accuracy degrades, so I would route in two stages, picking a tool group first, then the tool.

And measure it. Tool selection is a classification problem, so build a labelled set of queries with the expected call and score it on every prompt change. Otherwise you are tuning by anecdote.

Trap

Treating model-generated arguments as trusted because they came from your own model. They are the least trusted input in the system — an attacker controls them via prompt injection in any document the agent reads.

04

Streaming & time-to-first-token

On your résuméCore

Two different latencies. TTFT is how long until the first token appears; TPOT is how fast the rest arrives. Streaming attacks TTFT, which is the one users actually feel.

Think of it as

A kettle with a glass body. It boils in the same time either way, but watching it fill with steam is a completely different experience from staring at steel.

How it actually works
  • Prefill processes your whole prompt in parallel — cost scales with input length, and it sets TTFT.
  • Decode generates one token at a time, each attending to all previous — it sets TPOT and scales with output length.
  • So: a long prompt hurts TTFT, a long answer hurts total time. Trimming retrieved context is a *latency* fix, not just a cost fix.
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE) is the right transport — one-directional, plain HTTP, reconnects for free. WebSockets are overkill for token streaming.
  • Streaming changes error handling: you have already sent a 200 and half an answer when the failure arrives. You need an in-band error event, not a status code.
Template
pythonSSE streaming, including the mid-stream failure case
@app.get("/copilot/stream")
async def stream(q: str, request: Request):
    async def gen():
        try:
            async for chunk in agent.run(q):
                if await request.is_disconnected():
                    break                       # stop paying for a dead client
                yield f"data: {json.dumps({'t': chunk})}\n\n"
            yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
        except Exception as e:
            log.exception("stream failed")
            # Headers are long gone — the error must travel in-band.
            yield f"event: error\ndata: {json.dumps({'msg': str(e)})}\n\n"

    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")
They will ask

Because it is the one the user experiences as responsiveness. Total time to a 400-token answer is dominated by decode, which is bounded by the model — I cannot make it much faster. TTFT is dominated by my own overhead: polling, state fetches, prompt length, and tool round trips, all of which I control.

That is why I quote both. Dropping TTFT under a second changed how the feature felt; dropping end-to-end from 8–15s to 2–5s is the wall-clock claim.

You cannot change the status code — it was 200 the moment the first byte went out. So the contract has to carry errors in-band: a named SSE error event that the client listens for, distinct from the [DONE] sentinel.

On the client, partial output stays on screen with an explicit failure marker rather than vanishing, because silently discarding text the user already read is worse than showing it was cut short.

05

Percentiles: p50, p95, p99

On your résuméCore

Averages hide the users you are losing. p95 = 95% of requests were faster than this. In an interview, quoting p95 instead of "average" instantly reads as someone who has run a service.

Think of it as

Average income in a room with a billionaire tells you nothing about anyone in it. The median and the tail do.

How it actually works
  • A single slow dependency shows up in p99 long before it moves the mean — the tail is your early-warning system.
  • Percentiles do not add. You cannot sum the p95 of three services to get the p95 of the chain; the tail compounds worse than that.
  • Fan-out amplifies tails: if a request hits 10 backends, it is roughly as slow as the slowest, so a 1-in-100 slow backend affects ~10% of requests.
  • Report a window: "p95 over 7 days". A percentile without a time window is not a number.
  • Your 8-15s → 2-5s is really a range. Convert it: what were p50 and p95 before and after? That is the version that survives cross-examination.
They will ask

Tail latency is almost never CPU — it is queueing, contention, or a cold path. In order: garbage-collection pauses, connection-pool exhaustion, a cache miss falling through to a slow origin, a lock, or a retry storm from a downstream that just got slower.

The way to find it is tracing, not metrics. A metric tells you the tail moved; a distributed trace on the slow requests specifically tells you which span owns it. Sampling by latency — always trace the slowest 1% — is what makes that practical.

Trap

Being asked "was that p50 or p95?" and not knowing. Go and pull the real numbers from your dashboards before the interview. This is the single most likely place your best story gets punctured.

06

Feature flags & the flag-switchable rollback

On your résuméCore

A runtime switch that decouples deploying code from releasing behaviour. Both runtimes shipped in the same binary; a config change chose which one ran.

Think of it as

A double-track railway with a points lever. The new line is already laid and tested; switching traffic is a lever pull, not a construction project.

How it actually works
  • Why it matters: rollback becomes seconds instead of a 4–5 day hotfix cycle — build, review, QA, release train.
  • Granularity is the real design: global, per-tenant, or percentage rollout. Per-tenant lets you pilot with friendly practices first.
  • Kill switch vs experiment flag: a kill switch is permanent and must default safe; an experiment flag is temporary and must be deleted.
  • Flag debt is real. Two runtimes behind a flag means every bug reproduces twice and every test matrix doubles. Ship it, then set a date to delete the old path.
  • Evaluate flags once per request and pass the decision down — not scattered through the call stack, or one request can run half in each mode.
Template
pythonDecide once at the edge, then pass it down
def handle(request):
    # Resolve ONCE per request. Re-checking deeper down means a single
    # request can execute half old-path, half new-path.
    runtime = flags.variant(
        "copilot.runtime",
        default="assistants",         # safe default: the known-good path
        tenant=request.tenant_id,
        rollout={"agentic": 0.10},    # 10% of tenants, sticky by hash
    )
    engine = AGENTIC if runtime == "agentic" else ASSISTANTS
    with trace.span("copilot", runtime=runtime):   # tag telemetry with it
        return engine.run(request)
They will ask

Rolled out by tenant, not by percentage of requests, so a given practice always saw one consistent experience — mixed behaviour within one clinic's session would have been confusing and unsupportable.

Started with internal and a small pilot set, watched error rate and latency tagged by runtime so the two were directly comparable on one dashboard, then widened. The flag defaulted to the old path, so any failure to read config failed safe.

Doubled surface area. Every bug report starts with "which runtime", every integration test matrix doubles, and dead code rots because nobody is reading it. It is genuinely expensive.

It was worth it during migration because the alternative was a multi-day hotfix on a clinical feature. But a migration flag with no removal date is just permanent complexity — the correct end state is deleting the old path once confidence is there.

Say this

Both runtimes shipped in the same binary behind a per-tenant flag defaulting to the old path. Rolling back was a config change measured in seconds, not a hotfix measured in days.

//The Provisioning CLI

The Provisioning CLI

Your strongest self-initiated story: you found the problem, built the tool, and shipped it as a distribution channel rather than a script. That combination is exactly what a hiring committee reads as scope.

The line this defends

Cut dev-environment setup from 1-2 days and 3-4 engineers to a single 10-minute command with a self-initiated 12-phase idempotent provisioning tool, packaged as a versioned CLI so build-process changes reach all 40 engineers across India and US through one upgrade command.

01

Idempotency in provisioning

On your résuméCore

Running the tool twice leaves the machine in the same state as running it once. Every phase asks "is this already true?" before doing anything.

Think of it as

A packing list, not a set of instructions. "Passport in the bag" is safe to re-read; "put the passport in the bag" run twice packs two passports.

How it actually works
  • Declarative, not imperative: phases assert desired state (user exists, port 3306 responds) rather than performing actions blindly.
  • This is what makes the tool resumable. A laptop that dies at phase 8 re-runs and skips 1–7 in seconds — the difference between a tool and a script.
  • Idempotency is also what makes it safe to re-run for updates: the same command that installs also upgrades.
  • The hard cases are the non-idempotent primitives: appending to a config file, INSERT without a uniqueness constraint, generating a new secret. Each needs an explicit guard.
Template
pythonThe phase contract that makes the whole thing resumable
class Phase:
    name: str
    def check(self) -> bool:  ...   # is the desired state already true?
    def apply(self) -> None:  ...   # make it true
    def verify(self) -> bool: ...   # prove it, independently of apply()

def provision(phases, state):
    for i, p in enumerate(phases, 1):
        if state.done(p.name) and p.check():
            log.info("%02d %-24s skip", i, p.name)
            continue
        log.info("%02d %-24s ...", i, p.name)
        p.apply()
        if not p.verify():                     # never trust apply()
            raise PhaseFailed(p.name)          # stop; next run resumes here
        state.mark(p.name)                     # checkpoint to disk
They will ask

It was never one big task — it was a long tail of small unknowns. Undocumented tribal steps, versions that had drifted since the wiki was written, ordering dependencies nobody had written down, and secrets you had to ask a specific person for.

The cost multiplier was that it took three or four engineers, because a new joiner would get stuck and pull someone senior in. Encoding the knowledge into checked phases turned tacit knowledge into something executable, and the verify step meant it failed loudly at the right phase instead of silently three steps later.

You make the *outcome* idempotent even when the operation is not. For a secret, check whether one already exists in the store and only generate when absent — so the assertion is "a valid secret exists", not "generate a secret".

For appending to a config file, write a marker-delimited block and replace the block rather than appending. Same principle: convert the imperative action into a desired-state assertion.

Trap

Calling it idempotent when it is only "safe to re-run". Idempotent means the *end state* is identical. If a second run reinstalls and takes the same 10 minutes, it is re-runnable, not idempotent — know which one you built.

02

Shipping it as a versioned CLI

On your résuméCore

The insight that upgrades this from a script to infrastructure: packaging it means a build-process change reaches 40 engineers through one upgrade command instead of a Slack message nobody reads.

Think of it as

The difference between emailing everyone a recipe and opening a restaurant. One depends on 40 people doing it right; the other has one kitchen.

How it actually works
  • Semantic versioning: MAJOR breaks, MINOR adds, PATCH fixes. A provisioning tool's MAJOR bump means "your existing environment needs migration", which is a real user-facing contract.
  • Version pinning per branch: the tool version should be declared in the repo, so checking out an old branch provisions the environment that branch expects.
  • Self-update check on run — warn on drift, do not silently auto-upgrade. Silent upgrades break the one engineer mid-debug.
  • Telemetry: which version each engineer is on, and which phase fails most. Without it you are guessing where the pain is.
  • This is a distribution channel, and that framing is the senior signal. You did not automate a task; you built the path changes travel down.
They will ask

Same discipline as any API. Ship the new behaviour behind a minor version first with the old path still working and a deprecation warning naming the removal version. Give people a release where both work.

Then bump major, and make the tool detect an environment provisioned by the old major and either migrate it or fail with an explicit instruction. The failure mode to avoid is a half-migrated environment, because that is worse than either state.

The setup saving is one-off per engineer. The distribution channel is permanent. Before, any change to the build process was a message in a channel and a slow, uneven rollout where half the team was on a stale toolchain and nobody knew which half.

After, a build change ships as a version, and telemetry tells you adoption. That converts an unbounded coordination cost into a release.

Say this

The setup-time number is the headline, but the reason it mattered is that packaging it created a distribution channel — build-process changes now reach all 40 engineers as a version bump instead of a Slack message.

03

Self-initiated work — how to tell it

On your résuméCore

Nobody assigned this. That is the point, and it is the single hardest signal to demonstrate at L4 → L5. Tell it as: I noticed, I quantified, I built, I measured, it stuck.

Think of it as

The difference between a firefighter and someone who noticed the wiring and rewired the building. Only one of those gets promoted for it.

How it actually works
  • Noticed: be specific about the trigger — watching a new joiner lose two days is a better opening than "setup was painful".
  • Quantified before building: 1–2 days × 3–4 engineers × N joiners. Doing the arithmetic *first* is what distinguishes initiative from a side project.
  • Got buy-in: you cannot roll a tool to 40 engineers across two countries without persuading someone. Say who and how.
  • Measured after: 10 minutes, one command. And adoption — a tool nobody runs saved nothing.
  • Google's rubric calls this "scope beyond your assigned work". Say the sentence explicitly: *nobody asked me to build this.*
They will ask

It had to be strictly easier than the status quo on day one, so I made the first run work end-to-end before showing anyone — a tool that half works gets abandoned and never gets a second try.

Then I used onboarding as the wedge: new joiners had no habit to unlearn, so they were pure upside, and their setup time became the visible proof. Existing engineers came across when the build process changed and the tool was the only path that had the change. Being the distribution channel is what made adoption inevitable rather than voluntary.

Trap

Under-claiming. Engineers routinely describe self-initiated infrastructure work as "a small tool I wrote". Say the numbers, say nobody asked for it, and say how many people use it.

04

Reproducible environments: the alternatives

Deep

Expect the follow-up: why a provisioning CLI rather than Docker Compose, a devcontainer, or Nix? Having a real answer shows you chose rather than defaulted.

Think of it as

Furnishing a rented flat versus shipping a prefab room. Both give you somewhere to sleep; the trade-off is how much of the building you are allowed to change.

How it actually works
  • Docker Compose: great isolation, but a large legacy service stack in containers can be slow on macOS file mounts, and native tooling like IDE debuggers gets fiddly.
  • Devcontainers: Compose plus editor integration. Strong choice if the whole team is on VS Code, weaker if they are not.
  • Nix: genuinely reproducible, and a genuinely steep learning curve for 40 engineers.
  • Provisioning the host: best when the stack is heterogeneous and pre-existing — you meet the codebase where it is instead of containerising a decade of assumptions first.
  • The honest senior answer names the trade-off you accepted: host provisioning is less isolated and drifts more, which is exactly why the verify() step per phase matters.
They will ask

It is the better end state and I would not argue otherwise. The reason it was not the move here is sequencing: containerising a large existing stack is itself a multi-quarter project, and the pain I was solving was immediate.

Provisioning the host got setup from two days to ten minutes without requiring the codebase to change at all. The cost I accepted is weaker isolation and more environment drift, which is why every phase verifies its own state independently rather than trusting that it ran.

//The Debugging-Ticket Agent

The Debugging-Ticket Agent

A small system with a sharp idea: capture engineering knowledge at the moment it is created, when it is cheapest and most accurate.

The line this defends

Built an LLM agent that turns each debugging session into a labeled, structured ticket record (root cause, fix, rationale) and appends it to a searchable AppSheet log, capturing 100+ tickets a month across the billing team.

01

Structured output

On your résuméCore

Forcing the model to emit JSON that conforms to a schema, so the output is a record you can store and query — not prose you have to parse.

Think of it as

A form instead of a letter. The letter may be beautifully written; only the form goes into the database.

How it actually works
  • Constrained decoding / strict mode masks invalid tokens during generation, so the output is *guaranteed* parseable. That is stronger than asking nicely and retrying.
  • Design the schema for queryability: enums for root-cause category, not free text. Free text cannot be aggregated, and aggregation is the entire value of the log.
  • Keep an evidence field pointing at the source — the stack trace, the commit. Structured output without provenance is unverifiable.
  • Always allow "unknown". A model with no null option will invent a plausible root cause, which is worse than an empty field.
Template
pythonEnums for what you will aggregate, free text only for what you will read
SCHEMA = {
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    # Enum, not free text — this is the column you will GROUP BY.
    "root_cause": {"enum": [
        "config", "race", "null_deref", "schema_drift",
        "third_party", "perf", "auth", "unknown",
    ]},
    "component":  {"type": "string"},
    "summary":    {"type": "string", "maxLength": 280},
    "fix":        {"type": "string"},
    "evidence":   {"type": "string", "description": "trace or commit ref"},
    "confidence": {"enum": ["high", "medium", "low"]},
  },
  "required": ["root_cause", "summary", "fix", "confidence"],
  "additionalProperties": False,
}

rec = llm.extract(transcript, schema=SCHEMA, strict=True)
if rec["confidence"] == "low":
    rec["needs_review"] = True      # queue for a human, do not drop
They will ask

You do not, per record — so the design has to assume some are wrong. Three mitigations: a required confidence field with low-confidence records flagged for review, an unknown enum value so the model has an honest exit, and an evidence field so any record can be traced back to source.

Then measure it properly: hand-label a sample against the engineer who actually fixed the bug and report accuracy per category. Some categories are easy — a null dereference is obvious from a trace. Race conditions are not, and I would expect accuracy to be visibly worse there.

Because the value of the log is aggregate, not individual. "Schema drift caused 30% of billing incidents this quarter" is an actionable finding; a thousand uniquely-worded descriptions of schema drift is not.

Free text goes in the summary field, which humans read. Anything I want to count gets a closed vocabulary.

Trap

Saying "I asked it to return JSON". Prompting for JSON and *constraining* generation to a schema are different reliability classes. Know which one you used.

02

Capture at the moment of creation

On your résuméCore

The reason this works: engineers will never write up a debugging session afterwards, but they will let a tool do it while the context is still in their head.

Think of it as

A dashcam. Nobody writes an accident report from memory a week later, and if they do it is wrong.

How it actually works
  • The cost of documentation is not writing — it is the context switch. Removing the switch is the whole product.
  • Knowledge decays fast: the reasoning behind a fix is largely gone within days, even to the person who made it.
  • 100+ tickets a month is the real metric here, because it proves adoption. A knowledge base nobody feeds is a dead knowledge base.
  • The second-order value is search: the next engineer hitting the same symptom finds the prior root cause instead of re-deriving it.
They will ask

Two things, and I would be careful not to overclaim either. The measurable one is duplicate-debug avoidance — the same class of bug recurring and being re-diagnosed from scratch. To claim it properly I would track how often a search precedes a resolution.

The one I would argue for even without a number is aggregate visibility. Once root causes are a closed vocabulary you can see that a third of billing incidents trace to one cause, and that turns firefighting into a fix you can prioritise.

03

AppSheet as the store

Jargon

Google's low-code layer over Sheets. Chosen because the consumers are billing-team humans who need to search and filter, not engineers who need an API.

Think of it as

Putting the fire extinguisher where people actually stand, not in the technically optimal cupboard.

How it actually works
  • Be ready to defend it. The honest defence: zero infrastructure, zero access-provisioning, and the non-engineers who need it were already living in that surface.
  • Know the limits so you are not caught out: row limits, no real transactions, no complex joins, and latency that is fine for tens of thousands of rows and not for millions.
  • The migration path is obvious and worth saying — append to a proper store and keep AppSheet as a view once volume justifies it.
  • Append-only is the right model regardless of backing store: a ticket record is an event, not a mutable row.
They will ask

Because the users were not engineers. The value only exists if billing-team people search it themselves, and AppSheet gave them filtering and views with no access-provisioning and no UI to build.

I would move it the moment volume or query complexity outgrew it — the write path is append-only, so swapping the sink is a small change. But building a service plus an admin UI first would have delayed the thing that actually mattered, which was proving people would use it.

Trap

Being defensive about the low-code choice. Choosing the boring tool that fits the user is a senior decision — as long as you can name its limits and the migration trigger.

//The e-KYC Identity Platform

The e-KYC Identity Platform

Your largest shipped system by user count, and the one with the most interesting trade-off in it: a threshold that trades fraud against locking out real doctors.

The line this defends

Cut fraudulent accounts 67% with an e-KYC identity platform on AWS Rekognition (Java, 6 flows: signup, EPCS, admin and member self-verification): 60,000+ users onboarded, 83% demographic match, $100,000+ revenue.

01

e-KYC / identity proofing

On your résuméCore

Proving a remote person is who they claim to be: they photograph a government ID, then take a selfie, and you check the document is genuine, the faces match, and a live human is present.

Think of it as

A bouncer checking a licence. Is the card real, is it you, and are you actually standing here rather than holding up a photo?

How it actually works
  • Three independent checks, and weakness in any one breaks the chain: document authenticity, face match (selfie ↔ ID photo), and liveness.
  • Demographic match — the name and date of birth parsed off the document reconciled against what the user typed. Your 83%.
  • Identity Assurance Levels (IAL) from NIST 800-63: IAL1 self-asserted, IAL2 remote-verified with evidence, IAL3 in-person. Remote e-KYC targets IAL2. Naming this is a strong signal.
  • The genuinely hard part is not the tech — it is the threshold, because a false reject is a real doctor locked out of their own practice.
They will ask

It is a business decision expressed as a number, so I would frame it as the cost of a false accept versus a false reject. A false accept is a fraudulent account with prescribing capability. A false reject is a legitimate physician blocked at signup — churn, a support ticket, and a bad first impression.

In a clinical product with EPCS in scope the asymmetry favours strictness, but you cannot just crank it up: past a point you are rejecting real users for lighting and camera quality. So you set it high, and you build a manual-review queue for the band just below the threshold rather than hard-failing there. That converts false rejects into a slower path instead of a lost user.

Face matching alone compares two images — it cannot tell whether the selfie is a live person or a photo of one. Without liveness, the attack is trivial: take a picture of someone's ID and a picture of their photo.

Passive liveness looks for signals a replay lacks — texture, depth cues, screen moiré. Active liveness asks for a randomised challenge like turning your head. Active is harder to spoof and worse for accessibility, which is the same false-reject trade-off in a different place.

Trap

Quoting only the match rate. The interviewer's next question is the false-accept and false-reject rates, because that is where the actual engineering judgement lives.

02

AWS Rekognition

On your résuméJargon

A managed vision API. CompareFaces returns a similarity score between two images; DetectFaces returns attributes and quality metrics you use to reject bad captures before you ever compare.

Think of it as

Renting a forensics lab rather than building one. You send evidence, you get a confidence score, you still decide the verdict.

How it actually works
  • CompareFaces gives a similarity percentage, not a yes/no. You own the threshold, and therefore you own the outcome.
  • DetectFaces quality attributes (brightness, sharpness, pose, eyes-open) let you fail fast with a *useful* message — "too dark, try again" beats "verification failed".
  • Face liveness is a separate managed flow; CompareFaces on its own is trivially spoofable by a photo.
  • Managed-service trade-off worth naming: no model to train or host, but you inherit their bias profile, their pricing, and their region availability — and biometric data means data-residency questions.
They will ask

Three I would raise. Bias: published research shows face-matching accuracy varies across demographic groups, so a single global threshold can disadvantage some users — that argues for measuring reject rates by segment rather than only in aggregate.

Data residency and retention: biometric data is regulated separately from PHI in several jurisdictions, so you need to know whether images are retained and where. And vendor lock-in on a scoring surface — because if the threshold semantics change under you, your fraud rate changes without a deploy.

03

EPCS

On your résuméJargon

Electronic Prescribing of Controlled Substances. DEA-regulated, and it mandates two-factor authentication plus identity proofing before a provider can prescribe a controlled drug electronically.

Think of it as

A gun licence rather than a library card. The identity check is not a product decision — a federal regulator specifies it.

How it actually works
  • This is *why* the e-KYC platform had to exist: EPCS makes identity proofing a legal requirement, not a fraud-team preference.
  • Two-factor is mandated — something you know plus something you have (hard token or a trusted device), enforced at the moment of signing.
  • Logical access control and an audit trail on every controlled prescription are part of the rule.
  • The stakes explain the strict threshold: a fraudulent prescriber account is a controlled-substance diversion route, not a chargeback.
Say this

EPCS is the DEA rule for e-prescribing controlled substances — it mandates identity proofing and two-factor at signing. It's the reason the identity platform was a compliance requirement rather than a fraud optimisation.

04

Defending "cut fraudulent accounts 67%"

On your résuméCore

The most attackable number on your résumé, because measuring fraud you *prevented* is genuinely hard. Have the methodology ready.

Think of it as

Claiming a lock reduced burglaries. You can count broken windows; you cannot count the burglars who walked past.

How it actually works
  • Be exact about the denominator: 67% of *what* — flagged accounts, confirmed-fraud accounts, or accounts blocked at signup?
  • Name the measurement window and whether it is before/after the same period length. Seasonality in signups is real.
  • Acknowledge the confounder honestly: some of the drop is deterrence — fraudsters stopped trying — which you cannot separate cleanly from detection.
  • The strongest version quotes a rate, not a count: fraudulent accounts per 1,000 signups, before and after. That controls for signup volume changes.
  • If you genuinely do not know the methodology, find out before the interview or soften the claim. Never estimate it live.
They will ask

Confirmed-fraud accounts per thousand signups, comparing equal windows before and after rollout — a rate rather than a count, so it is not just a signup-volume artefact.

I would flag the honest caveat: part of that drop is deterrence rather than detection. Once verification is visible at signup, some fraudulent attempts never start, and there is no clean way to attribute between the two. The number is real; the mechanism is mixed.

Trap

Answering "the dashboard said so". Every number you print is a question you have volunteered. If you cannot describe the denominator and the window, cut the number rather than defend it badly.

//The Subscription & Metering Layer

The Subscription & Metering Layer

The bullet with the best judgement moment in it — you modelled the unit economics and found a case where the pricing model loses money, then built the switch before it happened.

The line this defends

Enabled $10M projected ARR building the subscription layer behind Copilot's Free and $75/provider/month tiers (trial credits, per-module usage deduction, HIPAA-compliant RBAC). Added an off-by-default per-token switch after modeling that heavy practices could outcost their flat subscription fee.

01

Metering & usage deduction

On your résuméCore

Counting consumption accurately enough to bill for it. The hard requirements are exactly-once accounting under retries and never letting a balance go negative under concurrency.

Think of it as

A prepaid electricity meter. It must not double-count when the reader reconnects, and it must not let you keep drawing power at zero.

How it actually works
  • Deduct on an idempotency key derived from the request, so a retried request does not double-charge. This is the single most important property.
  • Concurrency: two simultaneous requests at 1 credit remaining must not both succeed. Either an atomic conditional update (UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= cost) or a Redis Lua script — never read-then-write.
  • Reserve and settle: for LLM calls you do not know the true cost until the response completes. Reserve an estimate up front, settle the difference after — otherwise a user can start a huge generation with one credit left.
  • Emit events, derive balances. An append-only usage ledger is auditable and replayable; a mutable counter is neither, and finance will eventually ask you to explain a number.
  • Per-module deduction means the ledger carries a module dimension, so you can price and report per feature.
Template
pythonReserve → run → settle, all keyed for idempotency
def call_with_metering(tenant, module, req_id, est_tokens):
    # 1. Atomic reserve. WHERE clause is the concurrency guard: two racing
    #    requests cannot both pass it.
    ok = db.execute(
        """UPDATE balances SET reserved = reserved + :est
            WHERE tenant = :t AND (credits - reserved) >= :est""",
        t=tenant, est=est_tokens,
    ).rowcount
    if not ok:
        raise InsufficientCredits(tenant)

    try:
        resp = llm.call(...)
    finally:
        actual = getattr(resp, "usage", None)
        # 2. Settle exactly once. The unique key on req_id makes a retry
        #    a no-op rather than a second deduction.
        db.execute(
            """INSERT INTO usage_ledger (req_id, tenant, module, tokens)
                VALUES (:r, :t, :m, :n)
                ON CONFLICT (req_id) DO NOTHING""",
            r=req_id, t=tenant, m=module, n=actual.total if actual else 0,
        )
        release_reservation(tenant, est_tokens, actual)
    return resp
They will ask

Exactly one succeeds, and it must be the database that decides — not application code. A read-then-write is a lost-update race: both read one credit, both think they can proceed.

So the check and the decrement are the same atomic statement — an UPDATE ... WHERE credits - reserved >= cost where the row count tells you whether you won. In Redis the equivalent is a Lua script, since it executes atomically.

Reserve then settle. Reserve a conservative estimate against the balance before the call so a nearly-empty account cannot start an expensive generation, then write the actual usage to the ledger and release the difference when it finishes.

The settle must be idempotent, keyed on the request ID with a unique constraint, because the settle path is exactly where retries happen — a client reconnecting after a dropped stream should not be billed twice.

Auditability and recoverability. A ledger lets you answer "why is this number what it is" months later, replay to rebuild a balance after a bug, and give finance a breakdown by module without a separate reporting pipeline.

The balance still exists as a materialised value for the fast path — you just derive it from the ledger rather than treating it as the source of truth.

Trap

Describing deduction without mentioning concurrency or retries. Those two are the entire difficulty of billing; everything else is CRUD.

02

The per-token switch — unit economics

On your résuméCore

You modelled cost per practice against a flat $75/provider/month and found the tail: heavy users whose token spend exceeds their subscription. Then you shipped the mitigation off by default.

Think of it as

An all-you-can-eat buffet that is profitable on averages and ruined by one table. You do not close the buffet — you keep a per-plate price ready.

How it actually works
  • Gross margin per tenant = price − (tokens × rate) − serving costs. Flat pricing is a bet that usage distribution stays inside your margin.
  • Usage is heavy-tailed, not normal. The mean tells you nothing; the p99 tenant is where the loss lives. Model the tail explicitly.
  • Off by default is the important decision: you built the capability before you needed it, without changing anyone's pricing or trust.
  • This is the strongest *judgement* moment in your résumé — you were not asked to model this. Say that.
  • The alternatives you can name as considered: fair-use caps, soft throttling, tiering by volume, or per-seat limits. Each trades revenue predictability against user trust.
They will ask

Cost per practice per month is tokens consumed times the provider rate, plus serving overhead. Revenue is seat count times the flat fee. Margin is the difference, and the question is what fraction of the usage distribution lands below zero.

The key input is not the average — it is the shape of the tail, because usage is heavy-tailed. A handful of high-volume practices can consume many multiples of the median. Once you plot margin against usage percentile you can see the crossover point where a tenant costs more than they pay, and decide whether that is an acceptable acquisition cost or a leak.

Because flat pricing was doing a real job — it is predictable for the buyer, and predictability is a selling point in a market where practices budget tightly. Switching everyone to metered pricing to solve a tail problem would have damaged the majority to fix the minority.

Off-by-default meant the capability existed the day it was needed, per-tenant, without a code change under time pressure. The engineering cost was small; the optionality was the point.

Say this

Nobody asked me to model this. I ran cost-per-practice against the flat fee, saw the tail crossed into negative margin, and built the per-token switch off by default — so the lever existed before we needed it, without changing anyone's pricing.

03

RBAC — role-based access control

On your résuméCore

Permissions attach to roles, users get roles. In healthcare it is not a convenience feature — it is how you enforce HIPAA's minimum-necessary rule in code.

Think of it as

Hotel keycards. Housekeeping opens rooms and the linen store; the guest opens one room; neither opens the safe. Nobody hands out keys per person.

How it actually works
  • Authentication is who you are; authorisation is what you may do. Interviewers check you never conflate them.
  • RBAC vs ABAC: roles are coarse (biller); attribute-based adds context (biller AND same_practice AND business_hours). Healthcare usually needs at least a little ABAC — same-practice scoping is an attribute.
  • Enforce server-side, always. Hiding a button is UX; the endpoint must still refuse. This is the most common real vulnerability in an otherwise sound app.
  • Deny by default. New endpoints should be inaccessible until explicitly granted, not open until someone remembers to lock them.
  • Break-glass access — emergency override with mandatory justification and loud audit alerting — is a genuine healthcare requirement worth knowing.
Template
javaDeny-by-default, enforced at the boundary
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/billing")
public class ClaimController {

    // Deny by default: no annotation would mean no access, not full access.
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('BILLER') and @scope.sameTenant(#claimId)")
    @GetMapping("/claims/{claimId}")
    public ClaimView get(@PathVariable String claimId, Principal actor) {
        auditLog.record(actor, "READ_CLAIM", claimId);   // HIPAA: every access
        return service.view(claimId);                    // view, not entity
    }
}
They will ask

RBAC as the backbone, with attributes for the things roles cannot express. Roles capture job function cleanly — biller, provider, front desk, admin — and stay comprehensible to the customer's own administrator, which matters because they manage it.

But tenant scoping and patient-relationship checks are inherently attribute-based: a provider may read charts for patients at their practice, not all charts. Pure RBAC would need a role per practice, which explodes. So the practical answer is roles for capability, attributes for scope.

Trap

Saying "we hid it in the UI". If the endpoint answers, the control does not exist. Say where the check runs and what happens when it fails.

04

ARR, MRR and "projected"

On your résuméJargon

Annual Recurring Revenue — contracted subscription revenue annualised. Your $10M is *projected*, and that word carries all the weight.

Think of it as

A restaurant's takings if every booked table shows up. Real bookings, hypothetical dinners.

How it actually works
  • ARR = MRR × 12, counting only recurring subscription revenue — not one-off fees or services.
  • Projected means modelled from expected conversion and seat counts, not booked. Say the word out loud; do not let it be discovered.
  • Know roughly how the projection was built — addressable providers × expected attach rate × $75 — even if you did not build the model.
  • The defensible framing: you built the *mechanism* that made the revenue collectable. You did not personally generate it.
They will ask

No, and I would not claim that. It is a projection built by the business from expected seat conversion at $75 per provider per month. My contribution is the layer that makes that revenue collectable at all — tiers, trial credits, per-module metering, and the access control around it.

Before the subscription layer existed, there was no mechanism to charge for Copilot. That is the honest version of the claim.

Trap

Letting an interviewer believe you drove the revenue. Volunteer the word "projected" before they ask. Owning the limits of your own number is a credibility gain, not a loss.

//Support Endpoints & Least Privilege

Support Endpoints & Least Privilege

A small change with a large organisational effect, and the cleanest security-design story you have.

The line this defends

Removed 60-80% of developer support load by exposing read-only props endpoints to support agents, scoped at the API security layer so they see the failing step but never customer PII. Adopted team-wide after joint India-US review.

01

Least privilege

On your résuméCore

Give every actor the minimum access that lets them do the job. Support agents need to know *which step failed*, which is a completely different question from *what the patient's data is*.

Think of it as

A mechanic's diagnostic port. It tells them the fault code without unlocking the glovebox.

How it actually works
  • The insight is that the debugging signal and the sensitive payload are separable. Most support escalations need shape and state, not content.
  • Enforce at the security layer, not the handler. A filter or interceptor that applies to every route cannot be forgotten on the next endpoint someone adds.
  • Return a projection / view object, never the domain entity. Serialising an entity is how a field added six months later silently leaks.
  • Audit every access anyway. Non-PII today can become PII when someone adds a field; the log is what makes that detectable.
  • Read-only removes an entire risk class — no support action can corrupt state.
Template
javaExplicit projection, so new fields cannot leak by default
// Support sees the SHAPE of the failure, never the payload.
public record WorkflowProbe(
        String  workflowId,
        String  failedStep,
        String  errorCode,
        Instant occurredAt,
        int     payloadFieldCount,   // "11 fields present"
        boolean patientLinked        // yes/no, never who
) {
    // Built by hand from the entity. Adding a PHI field to Claim does not
    // change this record, so it cannot leak through this endpoint.
    static WorkflowProbe from(Claim c) {
        return new WorkflowProbe(
            c.getWorkflowId(), c.getFailedStep(), c.getErrorCode(),
            c.getOccurredAt(), c.getPayload().size(), c.getPatient() != null);
    }
}
They will ask

By making the safe thing structural rather than remembered. The endpoints return hand-built projection records, not domain entities — so a new PHI column on the entity does not silently appear in the response, which is the failure mode with entity serialisation.

On top of that, scoping is enforced in the API security layer as a cross-cutting filter, so it applies to routes added later by people who never read this design. And every access is audit-logged, because the point of the log is to catch the case where the first two controls were wrong.

Escalations from support to engineering per month, before and after, normalised against total ticket volume so it is not just a quiet quarter. The cleanest cut is escalations of the specific category the endpoints addressed, since the tool cannot affect the others.

I would state it as a range because it varied by category, and be explicit that it is escalation count rather than engineer-hours — hours would be the better metric and we were not tracking them at that granularity.

Say this

The realisation was that support did not need the data — they needed the state. So I exposed which step failed and the shape of the payload as an explicit projection, scoped in the security layer rather than per-endpoint, with every access audited.

02

Getting it adopted team-wide

On your résuméCore

A joint India–US review is the interesting part: you took a security-sensitive change through cross-timezone consensus and it became the team standard.

Think of it as

Getting a building code changed rather than getting one house approved. Slower, and every house after yours is safer.

How it actually works
  • Security changes need explicit review sign-off — this is a case where process is protection, and being the person who sought it is the signal.
  • Cross-timezone work is real collaboration evidence: written proposals, async review, decisions that survive without you in the room.
  • "Adopted team-wide" means it became a pattern, not a feature. Say the word pattern.
  • This is the bullet to use for Googleyness-style questions on influence without authority.
They will ask

The concern was the right one — any new read path into production data widens the attack surface, and reviewers were sceptical of exposing anything to non-engineers.

What resolved it was changing the shape of the proposal rather than arguing for it. I moved from 'these endpoints are safe' to 'PII cannot travel this path by construction' — explicit projections, enforcement in the shared security layer rather than per-endpoint, read-only, fully audited. Once the guarantee was structural instead of a promise about care, the objection had nothing to attach to.

//Ambient Capture & Clinical Notes

Ambient Capture & Clinical Notes

The highest user-visible impact on your résumé, and the one where the accuracy number needs the most careful handling.

The line this defends

Saved 10,000+ practitioners 2+ hrs/day at 95% note accuracy with Copilot's ambient capture, transcription and summarization pipeline on Azure OpenAI (versioned prompts, streamed responses, Redis caching).

01

The ambient scribe pipeline

On your résuméCore

Microphone in the room during a consultation → streaming speech-to-text → speaker separation → structured clinical note → physician edits and signs.

Think of it as

A court stenographer who also writes the judgment summary. The judge still signs it, and the signature is the whole point.

How it actually works
  • Stage 1 — capture: chunked audio streamed as it is recorded, so transcription overlaps the visit rather than following it.
  • Stage 2 — ASR: speech-to-text. Medical vocabulary is the hard part; drug names and dosages are where generic models fail.
  • Stage 3 — diarization: who spoke. Attributing the patient's symptom description to the doctor corrupts the note.
  • Stage 4 — summarisation: transcript → a SOAP note (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) — the standard clinical structure.
  • Stage 5 — human sign-off. Non-negotiable. The physician is legally responsible for the note; the system drafts, it never files.
They will ask

Not the summarisation — the transcription of medical vocabulary. Drug names, dosages and abbreviations are exactly where general ASR degrades, and they are exactly the tokens where an error is clinically dangerous. "Fifteen milligrams" versus "fifty milligrams" is a one-phoneme error with a real consequence.

Diarization is a close second. If the model attributes a symptom the patient described to the physician's assessment, the note is wrong in a way that reads perfectly fluently — which is worse than an obvious error, because nobody catches it.

Constrain the task and make verification cheap. The summariser is instructed to draft only from the transcript and to leave a section empty rather than infer — an omission is a visible gap the physician fills, an invention is a plausible sentence they may sign.

Then make review fast: link note content back to transcript spans so the physician can check a line without re-reading the visit. And the sign-off step is mandatory. The system produces a draft; a licensed human is the one who files it.

Trap

Do not describe it as automating documentation. It drafts; a licensed physician signs. Getting that framing wrong in a healthcare interview is a serious tell.

02

Defending "95% note accuracy" and "2+ hrs/day"

On your résuméCore

Both numbers need a definition attached. Accuracy of *what*, measured *how*, against *whose* ground truth — and hours saved measured against what baseline.

Think of it as

"95% accurate" on a translation could mean 95% of words or 95% of meanings. Those are wildly different claims.

How it actually works
  • Word Error Rate (WER) is the ASR metric — substitutions + insertions + deletions over reference words. Note-level accuracy is different and softer.
  • Options for what 95% could mean: physician accepted without edit, clinically-significant-error rate, or a rubric score. Know which yours is.
  • Not all errors are equal. A misspelled word and a wrong dosage are both one error. A serious answer weights clinical significance.
  • 2+ hrs/day is almost certainly self-reported by physicians, which is legitimate — say so. Documentation burden ('pyjama time') is genuinely measured that way in the literature.
  • The clean framing: "physician-reported time saved" and "note-level acceptance rate", each with its measurement method.
They will ask

I would want to give you the measurement rather than the headline: it is note-level, judged against physician-reviewed ground truth, not word error rate — WER is the ASR-stage metric and it is a different number.

And I would add the caveat that matters clinically: an aggregate accuracy figure weights a misspelling the same as a wrong dosage. The number worth optimising is clinically-significant error rate, and that is what I would track if I were designing the evaluation from scratch.

Trap

This is the second-most attackable number after the fraud figure. Go and confirm how it was actually measured before your interview loop starts.

03

Prompt versioning

On your résuméCore

Prompts are production code: version them, review them, tie each generation to the version that produced it, and roll them back like any deploy.

Think of it as

A recipe card in a restaurant. When a dish suddenly tastes wrong you need to know which version of the card the kitchen was using last Tuesday.

How it actually works
  • Store the version ID with every output. Without it, a quality regression is unattributable and undebuggable.
  • Prompts belong in version control, not a database row someone edits live — you want diffs, review, and blame.
  • Gate changes on an eval set. A prompt edit is a model change; shipping it untested is shipping untested code.
  • A/B by version to compare quality in production, the same way you would compare two service builds.
  • Rollback must be a config change, exactly like the runtime flag — same principle, same reason.
Template
pythonEvery generation carries the prompt version that made it
PROMPTS = load_versioned("prompts/")     # git-tracked, reviewed in PRs

def summarise(transcript, tenant):
    v = flags.variant("note.prompt", default="soap@v7", tenant=tenant)
    tmpl = PROMPTS[v]

    out = llm.complete(tmpl.render(transcript=transcript))

    # Version travels WITH the artefact. A quality regression next month
    # is only debuggable if you can say which prompt produced which note.
    store.save(note=out, prompt_version=v, model=MODEL_ID, at=now())
    return out
They will ask

You cannot tell by reading it, so it has to be an eval gate. A held-out set of transcripts with reviewed reference notes, scored on the dimensions that matter — omissions, invented content, and correct SOAP structure — run on every prompt change like a test suite.

Offline eval catches regressions; it does not catch distribution shift. So in production I would tag every note with its prompt version and watch the physician edit rate per version, because the edit rate is the honest signal — it is the users telling you the draft was wrong.

04

Redis caching in an LLM pipeline

On your résuméCore

Three distinct uses, and interviewers want to hear you distinguish them: conversation state, response cache, and rate-limit counters.

Think of it as

A chef's mise en place. Prepped ingredients within arm's reach so the expensive part — actual cooking — is not spent fetching.

How it actually works
  • Session/conversation state: replaces the server-side thread fetch. Sub-millisecond, and the reason the agentic runtime could be fast.
  • Exact-match response cache: hash the normalised prompt + model + prompt version. Skips the model entirely on repeats.
  • Semantic cache: embed the query and serve a cached answer if cosine similarity is above a threshold. Powerful and dangerous — near-miss questions get confidently wrong cached answers.
  • Rate limiting: token bucket counters, atomic via Lua.
  • The cache key must include the prompt version and model ID. Otherwise a prompt rollout serves stale outputs from the previous version. This is the bug interviewers look for.
  • In healthcare, never cache PHI-derived output across tenants. The key is tenant-scoped, always.
They will ask

It answers a question the user did not ask. Two queries can sit above your similarity threshold and still have different correct answers — 'what is the dose for an adult' and 'what is the dose for a child' are semantically close and clinically opposite.

So in a clinical context I would not use one on anything patient-specific. Where it is defensible is generic, non-patient content like documentation lookups, with a conservative threshold and the cached answer surfaced with its source so a user can see what it matched.

Normalised prompt, model ID, prompt version, and tenant. Dropping the prompt version is the classic bug — you ship a prompt improvement and users keep getting the old output from cache, so the rollout looks like it did nothing.

Tenant scoping is a hard requirement rather than an optimisation, because anything derived from PHI must not be reachable across tenants no matter how identical the prompt looks.

//Charm Assist & the Licence Reader

Charm Assist & the Licence Reader

Two shipped features that show range: a multi-tenant key-management problem, and a genuinely low-level computer-vision one.

The line this defends

Shipped Charm Assist, a BYOK GPT-4 integration across 4 clinical modules (referral, lab, encounter, general), to 50,000+ practitioners, and an AAMVA PDF417 license reader (Java, ZXing) to 100,000+ users.

01

BYOK — bring your own key

On your résuméCore
