Symptoms the user feels, and one leading indicator. So: p95 time-to-first-token above target, error rate above the SLO threshold, and escalation or fallback rate — because that one moves before anyone files a bug and it is the honest signal that quality has degraded.

Then two that are specific to this system: provider circuit-breaker state, since an open breaker means we are serving degraded responses and nobody would otherwise notice; and cost per request, because a runaway agent loop shows up as tokens-per-request rising long before it shows up on an invoice. I would not page on CPU or on raw request volume — those are diagnostic, not symptomatic.

//AWS & Infrastructure as Code

AWS & Infrastructure as Code

You built on AWS with Rekognition. Know the core services well enough to place them in a design, plus what IaC buys you.

01

The core AWS services

Core

You do not need certification depth. You need to place the right service in a design and know its one significant limitation.

Think of it as

Knowing which shop sells what on the high street, not the inventory of each.

How it actually works
  • EC2 virtual machines; ECS/EKS container orchestration; Lambda serverless functions (cold starts, 15-min ceiling, no persistent connections).
  • S3 object storage — cheap, durable (11 nines), eventually consistent for overwrites historically, now strongly consistent for reads after write.
  • RDS/Aurora managed relational; DynamoDB managed key-value with predictable latency but rigid access patterns you must design up front.
  • SQS queue, SNS pub/sub, Kinesis streaming log. ElastiCache managed Redis.
  • CloudFront CDN; ALB layer-7 load balancer; Route 53 DNS with health-check-based failover.
  • IAM is the one to actually understand: roles over long-lived keys, least privilege, and never an access key in code.
02

IAM & the shared responsibility model

Core

AWS secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it. IAM is where most real-world breaches actually originate — over-broad policies and leaked long-lived keys.

Think of it as

The bank guarantees the vault. Whether you left your safe-deposit key on the counter is your problem.

How it actually works
  • Roles, not access keys. An EC2 instance profile or an IRSA role for a pod gives temporary rotating credentials. A long-lived key in an env file is the classic breach.
  • Least privilege, deny by default. Start with nothing and add. Action: "*" in a policy is a finding, not a shortcut.
  • Resource-level scoping: s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket/tenant-42/*, not on the whole bucket.
  • Assume-role for cross-account access with an external ID. Never share credentials between accounts.
  • Separate accounts per environment — the strongest blast-radius boundary AWS offers, and it makes a prod-versus-dev mistake structurally impossible.
03

Infrastructure as Code

On your résuméCore

Infrastructure defined in version-controlled files and applied by a tool. Terraform declares desired state and computes the diff — the same declarative idea as your provisioning phases.

Think of it as

A blueprint rather than a memory of how the building was put up. You can rebuild it, review changes to it, and see who changed what.

How it actually works
  • Declarative: you describe the end state, the tool computes the plan. terraform plan shows exactly what will change before it changes.
  • State file maps your config to real resources. It is sensitive and must be remote and locked — two concurrent applies against a local state file corrupt your infrastructure.
  • Drift is manual change made outside the tool. It is why console access to production should be read-only for humans.
  • Modules for reuse across environments; variables and workspaces for the differences.
  • Idempotent by construction — re-applying an unchanged config is a no-op. Exactly the property your 12-phase tool has.
  • Terraform vs CloudFormation vs CDK/Pulumi: Terraform is multi-cloud and declarative; CDK/Pulumi let you use a real programming language, at the cost of making the diff harder to reason about.
They will ask

That is drift: real infrastructure no longer matches the code. The immediate danger is that the next terraform apply silently reverts it — possibly during an unrelated deploy, possibly reopening whatever the change was closing. And there is no review record of why it happened.

Prevention is structural rather than procedural. Human console access to production should be read-only, with changes going through the pipeline. Then run terraform plan on a schedule and alert on any non-empty diff, so drift is detected in hours rather than discovered during an incident. Break-glass write access should exist, but as an audited, time-limited exception.

//Linux & Debugging a Box

Linux & Debugging a Box

You list Bash and Linux. Expect one practical question: something is wrong on this machine, what do you type?

01

Processes, threads & signals

Core

A process has its own memory space; threads share one. Signals are how the kernel and other processes ask a process to do something — including to stop.

Think of it as

A process is a company with its own office; threads are employees sharing it. A signal is a note slid under the door.

How it actually works
  • fork creates a copy-on-write child; exec replaces the process image. Together they are how every process starts.
  • SIGTERM (15) is a polite request to exit — catchable, and where you run graceful shutdown. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught; the kernel just ends you.
  • Graceful shutdown matters in containers: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, then SIGKILL. Handle SIGTERM to drain connections or you drop in-flight requests on every deploy.
  • Zombie process: exited but its parent has not reaped it. Orphan: parent died, adopted by init. In containers, PID 1 must reap children or zombies accumulate.
  • OOM killer picks a victim when memory runs out, scored by usage. Your process can be killed for someone else's allocation.
Template
pythonGraceful shutdown — without this, every deploy drops requests
import signal, sys

shutting_down = False

def on_term(signum, frame):
    global shutting_down
    shutting_down = True
    # 1. Fail readiness so the load balancer stops sending new work.
    health.set_ready(False)
    # 2. Finish in-flight requests, then exit. K8s waits for
    #    terminationGracePeriodSeconds before SIGKILL.
    server.shutdown(graceful_timeout=25)
    sys.exit(0)

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, on_term)   # k8s sends this first
signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, on_term)    # ctrl-c locally
02

Debugging a box

Core

A known sequence: load, then memory, then disk, then network, then the process itself. Having a sequence is the signal — flailing is not.

Think of it as

A doctor's triage order. Pulse, breathing, bleeding — in that order, every time, so nothing gets missed.

How it actually works
  • Load and CPU: uptime (1/5/15-min load), top/htop. Load above core count means queueing. High wa means you are I/O-bound, not CPU-bound.
  • Memory: free -h. Look at *available*, not free — Linux uses spare RAM as page cache and that is healthy. Check dmesg | grep -i oom for kills.
  • Disk: df -h for space, df -i for inodes (full inodes with free space is the classic confusing outage), iostat -x for saturation.
  • Network: ss -tnp for sockets and states. Many TIME_WAIT is usually fine; many CLOSE_WAIT means your app is not closing sockets — a real bug.
  • Process: strace -p PID for syscalls, lsof -p PID for open files, /proc/PID/status for the details.
  • Logs last, not first: journalctl -u svc --since '10 min ago'. Establish the shape of the problem before reading text.
Template
bashThe first sixty seconds on a sick box
uptime                    # load avg vs core count -> is it queueing?
dmesg -T | tail -40       # OOM kills, disk errors, network resets
vmstat 1 5                # r=runnable queue, wa=io wait, si/so=swapping
free -h                   # look at AVAILABLE, not free
df -h && df -i            # disk full... or INODES full with space left
ss -s                     # socket summary; CLOSE_WAIT piling up = app bug
top -o %CPU -b -n1 | head -20

# Find what is actually eating the disk
du -xh / --max-depth=2 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20

# What is this process blocked on?
strace -f -p $(pgrep -f myapp) -e trace=network,file -T
They will ask

Inodes are exhausted. Each file consumes an inode regardless of size, so millions of tiny files — session files, cached fragments, unrotated log shards — can exhaust the inode table while leaving most of the blocks free. df -i shows it and df -h never will.

The fix is finding and clearing the directory with the file count, then addressing the cause: log rotation, a cleanup job, or moving ephemeral files off that filesystem. It is worth knowing because the error message points you at the wrong thing.

/Languages & Frameworks

Languages & Frameworks

Every word in your skills section, and the question each one invites. If you print it, an interviewer may pick it — so know the one hard thing about each.

6 modules · 26 concepts
//Python

Python

Your interview language for Google. Beyond syntax, know the GIL, the memory model, and why a mutable default argument is a bug.

The line this defends

Languages: Python, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, SQL, Bash

01

The GIL

On your résuméCore

One lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads are useless for CPU-bound parallelism and excellent for I/O-bound concurrency.

Think of it as

A kitchen with one chef's knife. Four cooks help enormously while things are simmering; they cannot chop faster than one person.

How it actually works
  • Released during I/O — file reads, network calls, time.sleep. This is why threads genuinely help an API client or a web server.
  • Held during pure-Python computation, so four threads doing arithmetic run no faster than one, and often slower from lock contention.
  • CPU-bound → multiprocessing (separate interpreters, real parallelism, IPC cost) or a native extension that releases the GIL — NumPy, and your Numba and Cython work.
  • I/O-bound → asyncio or threads. asyncio scales to far more concurrent connections because a coroutine is far cheaper than an OS thread.
  • Python 3.13+ has an experimental free-threaded build removing the GIL. Worth knowing it exists; not yet the default.
Template
pythonPick the model from the bottleneck, not from habit
# I/O-bound: threads work, GIL is released during the wait
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=32) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(fetch_url, urls))       # ~32x speedup

# I/O-bound at scale: asyncio scales further, coroutines are cheaper
async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as c:
        return await asyncio.gather(*[c.get(u) for u in urls])  # 1000s

# CPU-bound: threads DO NOT help. Separate processes do.
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(crunch, chunks))        # real parallelism
They will ask

Split it by bottleneck, because the two halves need opposite answers. The three API calls are I/O-bound and independent, so they should run concurrently — asyncio.gather or a thread pool, and that alone takes three sequential round trips down to one.

The parsing is CPU-bound, so threads will not help at all thanks to the GIL. Options there are a process pool if it parallelises cleanly, or pushing the hot loop into something that releases the GIL — NumPy, or Numba if it is numeric. I would profile before assuming the parsing is even the problem; usually the network dominates and the second half is not worth touching.

Trap

Saying "Python can't do concurrency". It cannot do CPU parallelism with threads. It does I/O concurrency extremely well. Getting this distinction wrong is a common tell.

02

Data structures & their real costs

Core

list is a dynamic array, dict and set are hash tables, deque is a doubly-linked block list. Choosing wrong turns an O(n) algorithm into O(n²).

Think of it as

A numbered shelf, a card index, and a double-ended queue at a counter. Inserting at the front of the shelf means shifting every book.

How it actually works
  • list: O(1) index and append, O(n) insert or pop at position 0 — the classic accidental quadratic in interview code.
  • dict / set: O(1) average lookup, insert, delete. Since 3.7 dicts preserve insertion order as a language guarantee.
  • deque: O(1) append and pop at *both* ends. The correct choice for a BFS queue or a sliding window.
  • heapq: a min-heap on a list. O(log n) push and pop. For a max-heap, negate the values.
  • tuple: immutable, hashable, so it can be a dict key. Counter, defaultdict and OrderedDict cover most of the rest.
  • String concatenation in a loop is O(n²). Build a list and "".join(parts).
Template
pythonThe four that cover almost every interview problem
from collections import deque, defaultdict, Counter
import heapq

q = deque([start])                  # BFS: popleft is O(1), list.pop(0) is O(n)
while q:
    node = q.popleft()

graph = defaultdict(list)           # no KeyError, no setdefault noise
for u, v in edges:
    graph[u].append(v)

freq = Counter(words)               # freq.most_common(3)

heap = []
for x in nums:                      # k largest in O(n log k), not O(n log n)
    heapq.heappush(heap, x)
    if len(heap) > k:
        heapq.heappop(heap)         # evict the smallest
03

Generators & iterators

Core

A function with yield returns a lazy iterator: it produces values one at a time and keeps its state between calls, so it never holds the whole sequence in memory.

Think of it as

A tap rather than a filled bath. You take what you need when you need it, and an infinite stream costs nothing to define.

How it actually works
  • Constant memory over arbitrarily large sequences. Reading a 50 GB file line by line is the canonical use.
  • Lazy evaluation — nothing computes until you iterate. Chain generators and the data flows through one item at a time.
  • Single-pass. Once consumed, it is exhausted. This surprises people who try to iterate twice.
  • Generator expressions (x*2 for x in xs) are the lazy form of a list comprehension. Use them inside sum() and any().
  • yield from delegates to a sub-generator — how you compose them without a manual loop.
Template
pythonA pipeline where nothing is ever fully in memory
def read_lines(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:              # file objects are already lazy
            yield line.rstrip()

def parse(lines):
    for line in lines:
        if line and not line.startswith("#"):
            yield json.loads(line)

def claims_only(records):
    for r in records:
        if r["type"] == "claim":
            yield r

# Nothing has been read yet. One record flows through at a time,
# so this works identically on a 50GB file and a 50 byte one.
for claim in claims_only(parse(read_lines("events.jsonl"))):
    process(claim)
04

Decorators & context managers

Core

A decorator wraps a function to add behaviour around it. A context manager guarantees setup and teardown even when an exception is raised.

Think of it as

A decorator is a coat over the same person. A context manager is a door that always locks behind you, even if you leave in a hurry.

How it actually works
  • A decorator is just f = decorator(f). Everything else is syntax.
  • Always use functools.wraps or you destroy the wrapped function's name, docstring and signature — which breaks introspection and framework routing.
  • Context managers implement __enter__ and __exit__; @contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator into one with yield as the boundary.
  • __exit__ runs on exception too — that is the whole point. Returning True from it suppresses the exception, which you almost never want.
  • Real uses: timing, retry, auth checks, caching, database transactions, temporary state, and acquiring locks.
Template
pythonThe two patterns, written correctly
import functools, time, contextlib

def timed(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)            # keep __name__/__doc__/signature
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        finally:                    # record even when it raises
            metrics.observe(fn.__name__, time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return wrapper

@contextlib.contextmanager
def transaction(conn):
    tx = conn.begin()
    try:
        yield tx                    # body of the `with` runs here
    except Exception:
        tx.rollback()               # __exit__ path on failure
        raise
    else:
        tx.commit()
05

asyncio & the event loop

On your résuméCore

Single-threaded cooperative concurrency. await yields control back to the loop so other coroutines run while you wait on I/O.

Think of it as

One waiter serving twenty tables. They never stand still watching a kitchen — they take the next order while the food cooks.

How it actually works
  • Cooperative, not pre-emptive. A coroutine only yields at an await. One blocking call freezes the entire loop — including every other request.
  • Never call blocking code in an async function. requests.get, time.sleep, or a synchronous database driver will stall everything. Use asyncio.to_thread if you must.
  • asyncio.gather runs coroutines concurrently — this is the mechanism behind parallel tool calls in your agentic runtime.
  • asyncio.wait_for applies a timeout. Every external call needs one.
  • async is not faster for a single request. It raises the number of *concurrent* requests one process can hold, which is a different win.
Template
pythonConcurrent with timeouts, and errors that do not kill the batch
async def call_tools(calls):
    async def one(c):
        try:
            return await asyncio.wait_for(dispatch(c), timeout=5.0)
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            return {"error": f"{c.name} timed out"}

    # return_exceptions=True: one failure must not cancel the others.
    return await asyncio.gather(*[one(c) for c in calls],
                                return_exceptions=True)

# WRONG: blocks the ENTIRE event loop, every request stalls
# time.sleep(1); requests.get(url)
# RIGHT:
await asyncio.sleep(1)
await client.get(url)                       # async client
await asyncio.to_thread(legacy_blocking_fn) # escape hatch
They will ask

Something blocking in the event loop on that endpoint — a synchronous database driver, a requests call, a CPU-heavy parse, or a time.sleep. Because asyncio is cooperative and single-threaded, that one call stalls every other in-flight request on the process, which is why the symptom is global rather than local to the endpoint.

I would confirm it by measuring event-loop lag, and asyncio's debug mode will log coroutines that occupy the loop too long. The fix is either an async-native client or pushing the blocking work to a thread with asyncio.to_thread so the loop stays free.

06

Mutable default arguments

Core

Default arguments are evaluated once, at function definition. A mutable default is shared by every call — the most famous Python gotcha and a common interview filter.

Think of it as

A shared notepad stapled inside the desk. Every visitor writes on the same page, and each one is surprised by the previous entries.

How it actually works
  • The default object is created once and lives on func.__defaults__ for the life of the function.
  • Always use None as the sentinel and create the mutable inside the body.
  • The same trap applies to class attributes: a mutable class attribute is shared by all instances.
  • Dataclasses catch it — a mutable default raises an error and forces field(default_factory=list).
  • It is occasionally used deliberately for caching, but doing so intentionally is rare and confusing.
Template
pythonThe bug and the fix
# BROKEN: one list, shared by every call, forever
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add(1)        # [1]
add(2)        # [1, 2]   <- surprise

# CORRECT
def add(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []       # fresh object per call
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
07

Memory: reference counting & GC

Deep

CPython frees objects the moment their reference count hits zero. A separate generational collector exists solely to break reference cycles.

Think of it as

A library where a book is reshelved as soon as the last borrower returns it — plus an occasional sweep for books two readers have lent each other in a loop.

How it actually works
  • Reference counting is immediate and deterministic — this is why with blocks and __del__ behave predictably in CPython.
  • Cycles need the collector: a.b = b; b.a = a never reaches zero. The generational GC finds and frees these.
  • Three generations: new objects are collected often, survivors less so. Based on the observation that most objects die young.
  • gc.disable() is a real optimisation for short-lived batch processes with no cycles.
  • Common leaks in Python: an unbounded cache or dict, a growing module-level list, and lingering references in closures or exception tracebacks.
//Java & the JVM

Java & the JVM

You shipped production Java — e-KYC, the barcode reader, Spring services. Expect JVM internals, HashMap, and concurrency.

The line this defends

Backend: Spring Boot, Java Servlets, JSP, Tomcat. Testing: JUnit.

01

JVM memory & garbage collection

On your résuméCore

Heap holds objects, stack holds frames and locals. The collector reclaims unreachable heap objects, and its pauses are what shows up as tail latency.

Think of it as

A workshop floor that gets tidied periodically. The tidying is fast, but everyone stops working while it happens.

How it actually works
  • Young generation (Eden + survivors) for new objects — minor GC is frequent and cheap because most objects die young. Old generation for survivors — major GC is rarer and expensive.
  • G1GC is the modern default: region-based, targets a pause-time goal. ZGC/Shenandoah are low-pause collectors for large heaps.
  • Stop-the-world pauses are the operational concern — a major GC pause is a direct p99 latency spike.
  • OutOfMemoryError usually means a leak (an unbounded cache, a static collection, unclosed resources) rather than genuinely insufficient memory.
  • Heap sizing: too small causes constant GC, too large causes long pauses. Measure allocation rate and pause time; do not guess.
They will ask

GC pauses first, because that periodicity is the signature. Turn on GC logging and correlate pause timestamps against the latency spikes — if a major collection lines up with each spike, that is the answer.

Then the question is why. Usually it is allocation rate: something is creating far more garbage than necessary, so the old generation fills and major collections come around often. Fixing the allocation is better than tuning the collector. If allocation is genuinely necessary, switching to a low-pause collector like ZGC or reducing heap size to shorten pauses are the levers. And I would rule out the non-GC causes with the same signature — a cache expiry cycle, a scheduled job, or connection-pool churn.

02

HashMap internals

Core

An array of buckets indexed by hash. Collisions chain into a linked list, and since Java 8 a bucket with more than eight entries becomes a red-black tree.

Think of it as

A wall of pigeonholes. Two letters for the same hole stack up; if one hole gets very deep, it is reorganised into a sorted index.

How it actually works
  • O(1) average, O(log n) worst case since Java 8's treeification. Before that, a collision attack could make it O(n).
  • Load factor 0.75: at 75% full it resizes to double capacity and rehashes everything — an O(n) operation you can avoid by sizing the map up front.
  • equals/hashCode contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes. Break it and lookups silently fail — the object is in the map and cannot be found.
  • Never mutate a key after insertion. Its hash changes, its bucket does not, and it becomes unreachable.
  • HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent writes could infinite-loop pre-Java-8. Use ConcurrentHashMap, which locks per bin rather than the whole map.
Template
javaThe contract, and what breaks without it
public final class ClaimKey {
    private final String tenantId;
    private final String claimId;

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof ClaimKey k)) return false;
        return tenantId.equals(k.tenantId) && claimId.equals(k.claimId);
    }

    // MUST be consistent with equals. Override one, override both —
    // otherwise two equal keys hash to different buckets and the map
    // silently fails to find an entry that is definitely in it.
    @Override public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(tenantId, claimId);
    }
}

// Fields are final: mutating a key after insertion changes its hash
// but not its bucket, making the entry permanently unreachable.
03

Concurrency: synchronized, volatile, executors

Core

synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility. volatile gives visibility only. Executors let you manage threads as a pool rather than by hand.

Think of it as

A lock on the door versus a window everyone can see through. One stops two people entering; the other only ensures everyone sees the same room.

How it actually works
  • volatile guarantees reads see the latest write and prevents reordering. It does not make count++ atomic — that is read-modify-write, three operations.
  • synchronized provides both mutual exclusion and a happens-before relationship. Coarse-grained; prefer java.util.concurrent primitives.
  • AtomicInteger/AtomicLong use compare-and-swap for lock-free atomic updates. Faster than synchronized under contention.
  • ExecutorService over raw threads — bounded pools, a queue you control, and graceful shutdown. An unbounded pool is a memory leak.
  • Deadlock needs four conditions; break any one. In practice: acquire locks in a consistent global order and use timeouts.
  • Virtual threads (Java 21+) make thread-per-request viable again for I/O-bound work — the JVM's answer to async/await.
Template
javaWhy volatile is not enough for a counter
// BROKEN: volatile guarantees visibility, not atomicity.
// count++ is read, add, write — three steps, interleavable.
private volatile int count;
public void inc() { count++; }        // lost updates under concurrency

// CORRECT: compare-and-swap, lock-free and atomic.
private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();
public void inc() { count.incrementAndGet(); }

// Bounded pool: an unbounded queue is a slow-motion OOM.
ExecutorService pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    8, 32, 60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000),                  // bounded: backpressure
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());      // shed by slowing caller
They will ask

Sufficient when the operation is a single read or a single write and you only need visibility — a boolean shutdown flag is the textbook case. One thread writes true, others need to see it promptly, and there is no compound operation.

Not sufficient for anything read-modify-write, which is where people get caught. count++ is three operations, so two threads can both read the same value and both write the same increment — a lost update, and volatile does nothing about it. That needs an AtomicInteger with compare-and-swap, or a lock.

04

Streams & functional Java

Core

A declarative pipeline over a collection: intermediate operations are lazy, a terminal operation triggers the work.

Think of it as

A conveyor with filters and stampers. Nothing moves until someone at the end starts collecting.

How it actually works
  • Lazy until terminal: filter/map build the pipeline; collect/forEach/reduce execute it.
  • Single use. A consumed stream cannot be reused — reuse throws IllegalStateException.
  • Optional for the maybe-absent result. Do not call .get() without checking; use orElse, orElseThrow or map.
  • parallelStream() is rarely the right answer — it uses the common ForkJoinPool, so one slow parallel stream can starve every other one in the JVM.
  • Readability is the real benefit. A stream that is harder to read than the loop it replaced is a worse solution.

JavaScript & TypeScript

You list both plus React, Vue and Node. The event loop and closures are the two things always asked.

The line this defends

01

The event loop, microtasks & macrotasks

Core

JavaScript is single-threaded with a queue. After each task it drains the *entire* microtask queue (promises) before taking the next macrotask (timers, I/O).

Think of it as

A receptionist who finishes every follow-up note from the current visitor before calling the next one in.

How it actually works
  • Call stack → microtasks → macrotasks. Microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) run before the next macrotask, always.
  • Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks, UI events.
  • setTimeout(fn, 0) is not immediate — it queues a macrotask, so every pending promise callback runs first.
  • An infinite microtask chain starves the macrotask queue entirely and freezes the page or the server.
  • In Node, process.nextTick runs before other microtasks — its own priority level, and a common source of confusion.
Template
jsPredict the output — the standard interview question
console.log('1');

setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);        // macrotask

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3')); // microtask

console.log('4');

// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2
// Synchronous code first (1, 4). Then the microtask queue drains
// completely (3). Only then does the next macrotask run (2).
// setTimeout(fn, 0) means "soon", never "now".
02

Closures

Core

A function keeps a live reference to the scope it was defined in, even after that scope has returned. It is how private state and most callbacks work.

Think of it as

An employee who keeps their office key after the office closes — and the room is still there, still with their things in it.

How it actually works
  • The captured variable is a live reference, not a copy. This is the source of the classic var in a loop bug.
  • let is block-scoped, so each loop iteration gets a fresh binding — which is why let fixes that bug and var does not.
  • Closures are how you get private state without classes, and how callbacks and event handlers keep context.
  • Memory implication: a closure keeps its entire enclosing scope alive. A closure over a large object in a long-lived handler is a leak.
  • Every React hook depends on closures — a stale closure over old state is the single most common useEffect bug.
Template
jsThe loop bug, and why let fixes it
// BROKEN: var is function-scoped. All three closures share ONE i,
// which is 3 by the time the timers fire.
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);   // 3, 3, 3
}

// FIXED: let is block-scoped — a fresh binding each iteration.
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);   // 0, 1, 2
}

// Private state via closure — no class needed.
function counter() {
  let n = 0;                             // unreachable from outside
  return { inc: () => ++n, get: () => n };
}
03

Promises & async/await

Core

A Promise is a placeholder for a future value. async/await is syntax over the same machinery — the function returns a Promise and await pauses without blocking the thread.

Think of it as

A collection ticket. You are free to do other things; you present the ticket when the item is ready.

How it actually works
  • Three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected. Settled once and immutably.
  • Promise.all fails fast on the first rejection. Promise.allSettled waits for all and reports each outcome — usually what you want for independent calls.
  • Sequential awaits in a loop are a performance bug when the calls are independent. Start them all, then await.
  • Always handle rejection. An unhandled promise rejection crashes a Node process by default in modern versions.
  • await inside a try/catch is how you handle async errors — the reason async/await is more readable than .then().catch() chains.
Template
jsThe accidental serialisation, and the fix
// SLOW: each await blocks the next iteration. 10 calls x 200ms = 2s.
for (const id of ids) {
  results.push(await fetchClaim(id));
}

// FAST: start them all, then await. ~200ms total.
const results = await Promise.all(ids.map(id => fetchClaim(id)));

// When one failure must not lose the rest:
const settled = await Promise.allSettled(ids.map(fetchClaim));
const ok = settled.filter(r => r.status === 'fulfilled').map(r => r.value);
04

TypeScript: types, interfaces & structural typing

Core

Static types erased at compile time. TypeScript is structurally typed — compatibility is decided by shape, not by declared inheritance.

Think of it as

A duck test with a checklist. If it has all the listed features it qualifies, regardless of its family tree.

How it actually works
  • interface vs type: interfaces can be reopened and merged (good for public APIs); type aliases handle unions, intersections and mapped types.
  • Structural typing: any object with the required properties is assignable. No implements needed.
  • Types are erased at runtime. They cannot validate an API response — use Zod or io-ts for runtime validation at the boundary.
  • any defeats the whole system. Prefer unknown and narrow it, which forces you to actually check.
  • Discriminated unions are the most valuable pattern: a literal tag field lets the compiler exhaustively narrow, catching unhandled cases at compile time.
Template
tsDiscriminated union — the compiler catches the missing case
type Result =
  | { status: 'ok';       data: Claim }
  | { status: 'notFound' }
  | { status: 'error';    message: string };

function render(r: Result): string {
  switch (r.status) {
    case 'ok':       return r.data.id;      // narrowed: .data exists
    case 'notFound': return 'No such claim';
    case 'error':    return r.message;      // narrowed: .message exists
    default:
      // Add a 4th variant and this line fails to compile — the
      // exhaustiveness check that makes unions worth using.
      const _exhaustive: never = r;
      return _exhaustive;
  }
}

01

Spring Boot: IoC, DI and beans

On your résuméCore

The container creates your objects and injects their dependencies rather than each class constructing its own. That inversion is what makes the code testable.

Think of it as

A staffing agency rather than each department hiring independently. You declare the role you need; someone else supplies a person — including a stand-in during a rehearsal.

How it actually works
  • Constructor injection over field injection. It makes dependencies explicit, allows final fields, and works without the container in tests.
  • Bean scopes: singleton is the default (one per context) — so a singleton bean must be stateless or thread-safe. prototype and request exist for the rest.
  • @Transactional wraps a method in a database transaction via a proxy. Two classic traps: it does nothing on self-invocation within the same class, and by default it only rolls back on unchecked exceptions.
  • AOP implements cross-cutting concerns — transactions, security, caching — via proxies. This is how @PreAuthorize on your support endpoints works.
  • Filter vs Interceptor: filters are servlet-level and see raw requests (good for auth and CORS); interceptors are Spring-level and know the handler.
Template
javaConstructor injection, and the @Transactional trap
@Service
public class ClaimService {
    private final ClaimRepository repo;      // final: cannot be null
    private final AuditLog audit;

    // Constructor injection: no @Autowired needed on a single ctor,
    // and the class is trivially testable with plain `new`.
    public ClaimService(ClaimRepository repo, AuditLog audit) {
        this.repo = repo;
        this.audit = audit;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void submit(Claim c) { repo.save(c); audit.record(c); }

    public void batch(List<Claim> cs) {
        // TRAP: self-invocation bypasses the proxy, so submit() runs
        // with NO transaction here. Move it to another bean, or
        // inject self, to keep the proxy in the call path.
        cs.forEach(this::submit);
    }
}
They will ask

Because it makes dependencies honest. A constructor signature tells you exactly what the class needs, so a class with eight constructor parameters is visibly doing too much — field injection hides that.

Practically it also lets fields be final, which rules out accidental reassignment, and it means the object can never exist in a half-constructed state. And it makes testing trivial: you construct the class with test doubles and no Spring context at all, whereas field injection forces you into reflection or a container just to write a unit test.

02

FastAPI & ASGI

On your résuméCore

An async Python framework built on ASGI, with Pydantic doing validation and OpenAPI documentation generated from your type hints.

Think of it as

A form that validates itself and prints its own instruction manual from the same definition.

How it actually works
  • ASGI vs WSGI: WSGI is synchronous, one request per worker at a time. ASGI supports async, WebSockets and long-lived connections — which is why streaming responses work.
  • Pydantic models are the contract: validation, serialisation, and the OpenAPI schema all come from one type declaration.
  • Dependency injection via Depends — clean for auth, database sessions and per-request context.
  • StreamingResponse is how you do SSE, which is exactly the mechanism behind your token streaming.
  • The performance trap: a blocking call inside an async def endpoint stalls the whole event loop. Use def (FastAPI runs it in a threadpool) or an async driver.
03

Django & the ORM

Core

Batteries-included: ORM, admin, auth and migrations out of the box. The ORM is the part that will be asked about, specifically the N+1 problem.

Think of it as

A flat-pack house with the plumbing pre-installed. Fast to raise; you must still know where the pipes run.

How it actually works
  • MVT (model, view, template) — Django's naming for MVC.
  • QuerySets are lazy — no SQL runs until you iterate, slice or call len(). That laziness is what makes N+1 easy to cause accidentally.
  • N+1 problem: one query for a list, then one per item for a related object. Fix with select_related (SQL join, for foreign keys) or prefetch_related (second query, for many-to-many).
  • Migrations are generated from model changes and version-controlled. Review them — the autogenerated one is not always the safe one on a large table.
  • Middleware is the request/response pipeline: auth, sessions, CSRF, and your own cross-cutting logic.
Template
pythonN+1: 101 queries versus 1
# N+1: 1 query for claims, then 1 per claim for its patient.
for claim in Claim.objects.all()[:100]:
    print(claim.patient.name)          # 100 extra queries

# select_related: a SQL JOIN. One query. For FK / one-to-one.
for claim in Claim.objects.select_related("patient")[:100]:
    print(claim.patient.name)          # 1 query total

# prefetch_related: a second query + Python-side join. For M2M / reverse FK.
for claim in Claim.objects.prefetch_related("line_items")[:100]:
    for item in claim.line_items.all():   # 2 queries total, not 101
        ...

# Only fetch the columns you need — matters on wide clinical tables.
Claim.objects.only("id", "status").filter(tenant_id=t)
04

Node.js & Express

Core

Single-threaded event loop with a libuv threadpool for filesystem and DNS work. Express is a thin middleware chain over it.

Think of it as

One very fast waiter plus a small back-office team for the tasks that genuinely need hands.

How it actually works
  • Single-threaded for your code, so CPU-bound work blocks every request. Offload to a worker thread or a separate service.
  • Middleware is an ordered chain — each gets (req, res, next) and must call next() or the request hangs forever.
  • Error-handling middleware has four parameters (err, req, res, next). That signature is how Express recognises it.
  • cluster or PM2 forks one process per core, since one Node process uses one core.
  • Streams are the idiomatic way to handle large payloads without buffering them into memory.
05

Servlets, JSP & Tomcat

On your résuméJargon

The legacy Java web stack under CharmHealth. Tomcat is the servlet container; a servlet handles requests; JSP is server-rendered HTML compiled into a servlet.

Think of it as

The building and its staff. Tomcat is the building with the front desk; each servlet is a clerk assigned to a counter.

How it actually works
  • Servlet lifecycle: init() once, service() per request (dispatching to doGet/doPost), destroy() at shutdown.
  • Thread-per-request: the container assigns a pooled thread per request. So servlets must be stateless — an instance field is shared across concurrent requests.
  • Connector thread pool (maxThreads) is the concurrency limit. Exhausting it queues requests — a classic Tomcat outage.
  • Session state lives server-side keyed by JSESSIONID, which is why sticky sessions were needed before shared session stores.
  • JSP compiles to a servlet on first request. Slow first hit; fine afterwards.
  • Be honest and specific: this is the legacy surface you maintained and extended, not something you would choose today.

Frontend

Listed on your résumé, so fair game — but expect a lower bar. Know React's model properly and be honest about the depth of the rest.

01

React: rendering, reconciliation & keys

Core

You describe the UI as a function of state. React diffs the new virtual tree against the previous one and applies the minimum DOM changes.

Think of it as

Submitting a revised document and letting an editor mark only the changed lines, instead of reprinting the whole thing.

How it actually works
  • Re-render ≠ DOM update. A component function re-running is cheap; only the diff touches the DOM.
  • Keys must be stable and unique among siblings. Using an array index as a key causes wrong state to stick to the wrong row when the list reorders — the classic React bug.
  • State updates are asynchronous and batched. Reading state immediately after setState gives the old value; use the functional form when the new value depends on the old.
  • useEffect dependencies: a missing dependency creates a stale closure over old state. Empty array means run once on mount.
  • useMemo/useCallback are optimisations with a cost. Applying them everywhere makes things slower, not faster. Measure first.
  • Controlled inputs — value from state, onChange updates it — is the standard form pattern.
Template
jsxThe two most common React bugs
// BUG 1: index as key. Delete row 0 and every row's state shifts
// onto the wrong item, because React matches by position.
{rows.map((r, i) => <Row key={i} {...r} />)}
{rows.map(r => <Row key={r.id} {...r} />)}      // stable identity

// BUG 2: stale closure. count is captured from the render where the
// effect ran, so this always increments from 0.
useEffect(() => {
  const t = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(t);
}, []);                                         // count not in deps

// FIX: functional update — no dependency on the captured value.
useEffect(() => {
  const t = setInterval(() => setCount(c => c + 1), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(t);
}, []);

Vue, jQuery, Handlebars, Bootstrap

On your résuméJargon

The rest of your frontend list. Know the one distinguishing idea behind each and do not overclaim depth.

Think of it as

Tools in a drawer you have used. You can name what each is for without claiming to be a carpenter.

How it actually works

  • jQuery: pre-framework DOM manipulation and AJAX. Imperative — you mutate the DOM directly rather than describing state. Legacy, but everywhere in older codebases.
  • Handlebars: logic-less server-side templating. Deliberately restricted so logic stays in the controller.

01

Testing: mocks, stubs & what to test

Core

Test behaviour, not implementation. A test that breaks when you refactor without changing behaviour is a liability, not a safety net.

Think of it as

Checking the car still drives, not that the mechanic used a particular spanner.

How it actually works
  • Stub returns canned data. Mock additionally asserts it was called. Fake is a working lightweight implementation (an in-memory repository).
  • Mock at the boundary — the HTTP client, the clock, the third-party SDK. Mocking your own internals couples the test to the structure.
  • PyTest fixtures for setup with scopes (function, module, session). parametrize to run one test over many inputs.
  • JUnit 5: @BeforeEach, @ParameterizedTest, and AssertJ for readable assertions.
  • Selenium for end-to-end browser tests — slow and flaky, so keep a handful on critical journeys only.
  • Postman for manual API exploration and collection-based smoke tests in CI.
02

Numba & Cython

On your résuméDeep

Two ways to make Python numeric code fast. Numba JIT-compiles functions to machine code via LLVM at runtime; Cython compiles annotated Python to C ahead of time.

Think of it as

Numba is a simultaneous interpreter who gets fluent after the first sentence. Cython is having the speech professionally translated in advance.

How it actually works
  • Numba: add @njit to a numeric function and it compiles on first call. Best for NumPy-heavy loops. Falls back to slow object mode if it cannot infer types — nopython=True makes that failure loud.
  • Cython: a superset of Python with C type declarations, compiled to a C extension. More control, more build complexity, works for non-numeric code too.
  • Both release the GIL (nogil in Cython, parallel=True in Numba) — which is how you get true multi-core CPU parallelism in Python.
  • The real speedup comes from typed loops. Vectorised NumPy is already C; Numba wins where you have a loop NumPy cannot express.
  • Profile first. Reaching for a JIT before knowing where the time goes is how people optimise 3% of the runtime.
Template
pythonThe loop NumPy cannot vectorise — where a JIT earns its place
from numba import njit

@njit(cache=True)          # nopython by default; cache the compile
def max_drawdown(prices):
    peak = prices[0]
    worst = 0.0
    for p in prices:       # sequential dependency: NumPy can't vectorise
        if p > peak:
            peak = p
        dd = (peak - p) / peak
        if dd > worst:
            worst = dd
    return worst

# First call compiles (~100ms), subsequent calls run at C speed.
# Pure Python: ~2s on 10M points. njit: ~15ms.
03

Regex: greedy, lazy & catastrophic backtracking

On your résuméCore

Quantifiers are greedy by default — they take as much as possible then give back. Nested quantifiers on overlapping patterns can make matching exponential.

Think of it as

Someone who grabs the whole buffet then returns items one at a time until the plate fits. With two of them negotiating, it can take forever.

How it actually works
  • **Greedy .* vs lazy .*?** — greedy matches to the end of the line then backtracks; lazy matches as little as possible then expands.
  • Catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS): patterns like (a+)+$ on a non-matching string try exponentially many splits. A user-supplied regex or input is a denial-of-service vector.
  • Prevention: avoid nested quantifiers over overlapping character classes, anchor patterns, prefer specific classes to ., and set a timeout where the engine supports it.
  • Use non-capturing groups (?:...) when you do not need the capture — cheaper and clearer.
  • Compile once at module level rather than inside a loop.
  • Know when to stop: parsing HTML or nested structures with regex is the wrong tool. Say so.
Template
pythonGreedy vs lazy, and the pattern that hangs
import re

s = '<a><b>'
re.match(r'<.*>',  s).group()      # '<a><b>'  greedy: to the last >
re.match(r'<.*?>', s).group()      # '<a>'     lazy: to the first >

# CATASTROPHIC: nested quantifier over overlapping classes.
# On 30 a's with no trailing b, this tries 2^30 ways to split.
# re.match(r'(a+)+b', 'a' * 30)    # hangs

# SAFE: no ambiguity in how the input can be divided.
re.match(r'a+b', 'a' * 30)

CLAIM_RE = re.compile(r'^CLM\d{8}$')   # compile once, anchored, specific
04

OpenCV & ZXing

On your résuméJargon

The vision half of your barcode work. OpenCV does image preprocessing; ZXing does the actual barcode decoding.

Think of it as

Cleaning and straightening a photograph before handing it to someone who reads the handwriting.

How it actually works
  • OpenCV for preprocessing: greyscale, adaptive thresholding, deskew, denoise, perspective correction. Most decode failures are capture-quality failures, so this is where the wins are.
  • ZXing ('zebra crossing') decodes many symbologies. You give it a BinaryBitmap; hints let you restrict to PDF_417 and enable TRY_HARDER.
  • TRY_HARDER trades speed for a better chance on poor images — worth it for a one-off scan, not for a video stream.
  • Real-world failures: hologram glare, card curvature, low light, and motion blur. Guiding the capture beats improving the decoder.
  • Decode and parse are separate problems. ZXing gives you a string; the AAMVA parsing is yours, and that is where the version drift lives.

01

Joins

Core

INNER keeps only matches; LEFT keeps everything from the left; RIGHT the mirror; FULL keeps everything. The join condition decides correctness, the WHERE clause can silently undo it.

Think of it as

Two guest lists stapled together. Inner keeps people on both; left keeps everyone from yours regardless of whether they made theirs.

How it actually works
  • INNER JOIN: rows matching in both tables.
  • LEFT JOIN: all left rows; unmatched right columns are NULL. This is how you find *missing* records — LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL.
  • The classic bug: putting a condition on the right table in WHERE instead of ON turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN, because NULL fails the predicate.
  • CROSS JOIN is the Cartesian product — usually accidental, and catastrophic on large tables.
  • Self-join for hierarchies (employee → manager). USING(col) is shorthand when the column names match.
Template
sqlThe LEFT JOIN trap, and finding what is missing
-- BUG: this is now an INNER JOIN. Rows with no matching claim have
-- c.status = NULL, and NULL = 'paid' is never true, so they vanish.
SELECT p.id, c.status
  FROM patients p
  LEFT JOIN claims c ON c.patient_id = p.id
 WHERE c.status = 'paid';

-- CORRECT: filter in the JOIN condition to keep the outer semantics.
SELECT p.id, c.status
  FROM patients p
  LEFT JOIN claims c ON c.patient_id = p.id AND c.status = 'paid';

-- Anti-join: patients who have never submitted a claim.
SELECT p.id
  FROM patients p
  LEFT JOIN claims c ON c.patient_id = p.id
 WHERE c.id IS NULL;
02

Indexes & EXPLAIN

Core

An index is a sorted structure that turns a full scan into a lookup. EXPLAIN shows what the planner will actually do — read it before changing anything.

Think of it as

The index at the back of a book. It costs pages and must be updated on every reprint, and it turns a cover-to-cover search into a page number.

How it actually works
  • Composite index column order matters — the leftmost-prefix rule. An index on (tenant_id, status, created_at) serves queries filtering on tenant_id, or tenant_id + status, but not status alone.
  • A function on the column kills the index. WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026 cannot use an index on created_at; a range predicate can. Same for LIKE '%foo' with a leading wildcard.
  • Covering index: if the index contains every column the query needs, the table is never touched. In MySQL's EXPLAIN this shows as Using index.
  • Selectivity matters. An index on a boolean is usually useless — the planner will prefer a scan.
  • Every index costs writes. Unused indexes are pure tax on every insert and update; find and drop them.
  • Read EXPLAIN for: access type (ALL is a full scan), rows examined versus returned, and whether it says Using filesort or Using temporary.
Template
sqlLeftmost prefix, and the predicate that disables an index
CREATE INDEX idx_claims ON claims (tenant_id, status, created_at);

-- USES the index (leftmost prefix satisfied)
WHERE tenant_id = 42
WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND status = 'denied'
WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND status = 'denied' AND created_at > '2026-01-01'

-- DOES NOT use it (skips the leading column)
WHERE status = 'denied'

-- KILLS the index: the function hides the column from the planner
WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026
-- REWRITE as a range so the index can be used
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...;   -- read type, rows, and extra BEFORE tuning
They will ask

No — indexes are a read optimisation paid for on every write. Each one is another structure to maintain on insert, update and delete, plus storage and memory, so a table with fifteen indexes has a write path several times more expensive than it needs.

I would index from the actual query patterns: the columns in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY, as composites in the order the leftmost-prefix rule requires. And I would periodically look for unused indexes and drop them, because they accumulate — someone adds one for a report that was decommissioned a year ago and nobody removes it.

03

GROUP BY, HAVING & window functions

Core

GROUP BY collapses rows into aggregates; HAVING filters those aggregates. Window functions compute across a set of rows *without* collapsing them.

Think of it as

GROUP BY gives you the class averages. A window function writes each student's rank next to their own name, with the whole class still visible.

How it actually works
  • WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. Putting an aggregate in WHERE is an error.
  • Window functions — ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), LAG(), SUM() OVER (...) — keep every row. This is the modern answer to 'top N per group'.
  • PARTITION BY is GROUP BY for windows; ORDER BY inside OVER defines the running order.
  • ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK: ties get distinct numbers, gapped ranks, or unbroken ranks respectively.
  • Common table expressions (WITH) make multi-step queries readable and are how you write recursive queries for hierarchies.
Template
sqlTop N per group — the classic window-function question
-- The 3 most recent claims per tenant, without a correlated subquery.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT c.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY tenant_id            -- restart per tenant
           ORDER BY created_at DESC          -- newest first
         ) AS rn
    FROM claims c
   WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'          -- filter BEFORE the window
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;

-- Running total that keeps every row visible.
SELECT tenant_id, occurred_at, tokens,
       SUM(tokens) OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_id ORDER BY occurred_at)
         AS running_tokens
  FROM usage_ledger;
04

Normalisation & when to denormalise

Core

Normalisation removes duplicated data so one fact lives in one place. Denormalisation deliberately duplicates it to avoid a join — a read optimisation with a write cost.

Think of it as

One address book everyone references, versus writing the address on every envelope. The second is faster to post and wrong the moment someone moves.

How it actually works
  • 1NF atomic values, 2NF no partial dependency on part of a composite key, 3NF no transitive dependency. In practice: 3NF as the default.
  • The point of normalisation is update integrity — one place to change means no possibility of inconsistency.
  • Denormalise when reads vastly outnumber writes, the join is measurably expensive, and you can keep the copy in sync — via triggers, application logic or a materialised view.
  • Materialised views are managed denormalisation with a refresh policy. Usually a better answer than hand-maintained copies.
  • In clinical data, integrity wins. A denormalised allergy list that drifts is a patient-safety issue, not a performance trade.
05

Transactions & deadlocks

Core

A transaction is all-or-nothing. A deadlock is two transactions each holding what the other needs, and the database resolves it by killing one.

Think of it as

Two people in a corridor each stepping aside the same way, forever. Someone has to be told to go back.

How it actually works
  • Deadlocks need four conditions — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption, circular wait. Break any one and they cannot occur.
  • The practical fix is consistent lock ordering. If every transaction touches tables in the same order, a cycle is impossible.
  • Keep transactions short. Never hold a transaction open across a network call to a third party — that is how a slow API becomes a database outage.
  • Databases detect and kill a victim, returning a deadlock error. Your application should retry — deadlocks are expected, not exceptional.
  • Lock escalation and gap locks in MySQL's REPEATABLE READ can lock more rows than you expect, which surprises people migrating from Postgres.
They will ask

Read the deadlock log first — both MySQL and Postgres report the two transactions and the locks involved, so you can see the actual cycle rather than theorise about it.

The fix is almost always consistent lock ordering: if one code path updates claims then patients and another does the reverse, they will eventually meet. Making every path acquire in the same order removes the cycle entirely. Alongside that: shorten transactions so the window for collision is smaller, take the narrowest lock that works, and add bounded retry with jitter, because under concurrency some deadlocks are normal and a retry is the correct response rather than an error to surface.

//MySQL, MongoDB & Redis

MySQL, MongoDB & Redis

The three stores on your résumé. Know the storage engine, the document model, and Redis's persistence and eviction behaviour.

01

MySQL & InnoDB

On your résuméCore

InnoDB stores rows inside the primary key's B+tree — the table *is* the clustered index. Every secondary index stores the primary key, not a row pointer.

Think of it as

A filing cabinet where the folders are physically ordered by ID. Any other index is a card that gives you the ID, so you still walk to the drawer.

How it actually works
  • Clustered index: rows are stored in primary-key order. This makes PK range scans fast and makes the PK choice consequential.
  • Secondary index lookups cost two traversals — index to PK, then PK to row. A covering index avoids the second.
  • Choose a small, monotonically increasing PK. A random UUID as a clustered key causes page splits and bloats every secondary index. Use an auto-increment BIGINT or a time-ordered UUIDv7.
  • MVCC via undo logs gives consistent reads without blocking writers. Default isolation is REPEATABLE READ, unlike Postgres's READ COMMITTED.
  • Replication is logical (binlog) — statement, row, or mixed. Row-based is safer and the modern default.
  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes row locks; under REPEATABLE READ it may also take gap locks, which lock ranges you did not expect.
They will ask

Because the primary key defines physical row order. An auto-increment key appends to the end of the B+tree, which is sequential and cache-friendly. A random UUID inserts into the middle of the tree, causing page splits, fragmentation and far more random I/O.

It compounds too: every secondary index stores the primary key as its pointer, so a 16-byte random key makes every index on the table bigger and less cacheable. If I need globally unique IDs I would use a time-ordered scheme like UUIDv7 or ULID, which keeps insertion sequential while staying unique.

02

MongoDB

On your résuméCore

Document store — BSON documents in collections, no enforced schema by default. The design question is always embed or reference.

Think of it as

A folder per case with everything stapled inside, rather than sheets filed across many cabinets.

How it actually works
  • Embed when data is accessed together and is bounded — one round trip, atomic per document. Reference when data is shared, unbounded, or updated independently.
  • The 16MB document limit is the hard constraint that kills naive embedding of an unbounded array.
  • Indexes work like any B-tree — compound indexes follow the same leftmost-prefix rule as SQL.
  • Aggregation pipeline ($match, $group, $lookup, $project) is the query language for anything beyond a find. Put $match first so it can use an index.
  • Multi-document transactions exist since 4.0 but are more expensive than in a relational store — if you need them constantly, the data model is wrong.
  • Write concern (w: majority) and read concern are your durability and consistency dials. Defaults are not always what you want.
They will ask

Embed, given the access pattern. Line items are always read with their claim, they are bounded — tens, not thousands — and they change with the claim, so embedding gives one round trip and atomic updates without a transaction.

I would reference instead if the array were unbounded, since documents cap at 16MB and an ever-growing array also causes the document to be rewritten and relocated on every append. Also if line items were queried independently across claims, or shared between documents. The rule I would state is: embed for contains-and-bounded, reference for shared-or-unbounded.

03

Redis: data types & persistence

On your résuméCore

An in-memory data-structure server, single-threaded for commands so every operation is atomic. Persistence is optional and comes in two flavours.

Think of it as

A whiteboard next to the filing cabinet. Instant to read and write, and you must decide how often to photograph it.

How it actually works
  • Types: String, Hash (objects), List (queues), Set, Sorted Set (leaderboards, rate limits, delayed queues), plus Streams, HyperLogLog and Bitmaps.
  • Single-threaded command execution means individual commands are atomic — no locking needed. It also means one slow command (KEYS * on a large database) blocks everything.
  • RDB: point-in-time snapshots. Compact, fast restart, loses writes since the last snapshot. AOF: append-only command log. More durable, larger, slower restart.
  • Redis can lose data. Even AOF with everysec can lose a second. Never use it as the source of truth for money — which is exactly why your billing ledger lives in Postgres.
  • Eviction policies: allkeys-lru for a pure cache, volatile-ttl when only some keys should expire, noeviction (the default) which starts erroring on write when memory fills.
  • Lua scripts execute atomically — how you do check-and-decrement for rate limiting and credit deduction in one round trip.
Template
pythonSorted sets: rate windows, leaderboards and delayed queues
# Sliding-window rate limit with a sorted set scored by timestamp.
now = time.time()
pipe = r.pipeline()
pipe.zremrangebyscore(key, 0, now - WINDOW)   # drop expired entries
pipe.zcard(key)                              # how many left in window
pipe.zadd(key, {str(uuid4()): now})
pipe.expire(key, WINDOW)
_, count, _, _ = pipe.execute()
allowed = count < LIMIT

# Delayed queue: score = when it should run.
r.zadd("due", {job_id: run_at_epoch})
due_now = r.zrangebyscore("due", 0, time.time(), start=0, num=10)

# NEVER on a large database: O(n), blocks the single thread.
# r.keys("claim:*")        ->  use SCAN with a cursor instead
They will ask

It depends entirely on maxmemory-policy, and the default surprises people: noeviction means writes start returning errors while reads keep working. If Redis is your cache, that is the wrong behaviour — you want it to evict rather than fail.

So for a cache I would set allkeys-lru, which evicts the least recently used regardless of TTL. volatile-lru only evicts keys that have a TTL, which is right when the instance mixes cache data with data that must not disappear — though mixing those in one instance is itself something I would avoid. And I would alert on memory usage and eviction rate, because a rising eviction rate means the working set has outgrown the instance and hit rate is quietly collapsing.

//NumPy, Pandas & Scraping

NumPy, Pandas & Scraping

The data-handling tail of your skills list. One or two questions deep, mostly about vectorisation.

01

NumPy & vectorisation

On your résuméCore

A contiguous typed array with operations implemented in C. Vectorising means expressing a loop as an array operation so the loop runs in C, not Python.

Think of it as

Telling the whole class to turn the page, instead of walking to each desk in turn.

How it actually works
  • Why it is fast: contiguous memory, one dtype, no per-element Python object overhead, and SIMD instructions.
  • Broadcasting lets arrays of different shapes combine without copying — arr - arr.mean(axis=0) works because the row vector is stretched implicitly.
  • Views versus copies: slicing returns a *view* sharing memory. Mutating a slice mutates the original — a real source of bugs. .copy() when you need independence.
  • Avoid Python loops over arrays. A vectorised operation is typically 10–100× faster than the equivalent for loop.
  • This is where Numba fits: when the loop has a sequential dependency NumPy cannot express.
02

Pandas

On your résuméCore

Labelled tabular data on top of NumPy. The DataFrame is a dict of columns, each a typed array — which explains most of its performance behaviour.

Think of it as

A spreadsheet with a programming interface — and the same trap, where a formula dragged down a million rows is slow.

How it actually works
  • Column-oriented. Operating on a column is fast; iterating rows with iterrows() is very slow and almost always avoidable.
  • apply is a disguised loop. Prefer vectorised operations; use np.where or .map on a dict for conditionals.
  • groupby().agg() is the workhorse — split, apply, combine. Same mental model as SQL's GROUP BY.
  • merge is a SQL join with the same semantics; watch out for duplicated keys silently multiplying rows.
  • SettingWithCopyWarning means you may be writing to a view, not the frame. Use .loc[row, col] = value to be explicit.
  • Memory: an object dtype column stores Python objects. Convert repeated strings to category for large frames.
03

BeautifulSoup & scraping ethics

On your résuméJargon

An HTML parser that tolerates malformed markup. The engineering question is rarely the parsing — it is rate limiting, robustness and whether you should be scraping at all.

Think of it as

Reading a badly photocopied form. The reader copes with the smudges; the real question is whether you were given permission to read it.

How it actually works
  • Parser choice matters: html.parser is built in, lxml is much faster, html5lib is the most lenient and the slowest.
  • Select by structure, not by brittle full paths. CSS selectors on stable attributes survive markup changes; a long chain of div > div > span does not.
  • Scrapers break constantly — sites change. Fail loudly with a clear error rather than silently returning None and poisoning downstream data.
  • Be a good citizen: respect robots.txt, rate-limit, identify yourself in the user agent, and cache so you do not refetch.
  • Prefer an API if one exists. Saying this first in an interview signals judgement, not just capability.
04

Schema design in practice

On your résuméCore

The decisions that are expensive to reverse: primary keys, tenant scoping, soft deletes, temporal data, and where you put the audit trail.

Think of it as

The foundations. Everything else can be renovated; these cannot without moving out.

How it actually works
  • Every multi-tenant table carries tenant_id, and it is the leading column of most indexes. This is a correctness constraint, not a convenience.
  • Soft delete (deleted_at) over hard delete in regulated data — but every query must then filter it, so enforce that in the data layer, not by convention.
  • Append-only for anything auditable. Clinical notes and usage ledgers are amended or superseded, never updated in place.
  • Store timestamps in UTC with a timezone-aware type. Then store the originating timezone separately if it matters clinically — 'the morning dose' depends on the patient's local time.
  • Money and quantities: DECIMAL, never floating point. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 is a real billing bug.
  • Constraints are documentation the database enforces. Foreign keys, unique constraints and check constraints prevent whole categories of data corruption that application code will eventually let through.
They will ask

Versioned and append-only, never updated in place, because the prior version is legally part of the record — an amendment has to preserve what was originally signed.

Concretely: a note row for identity, and a note_version table holding each revision with its author, timestamp, signed status and content, plus a pointer to the current version for the fast read path. Signing creates an immutable version; amending creates a new one that references the previous. That gives you the audit trail for free rather than bolting it on, and it means the 'current' query stays a single indexed lookup instead of a scan over history.

/CS Fundamentals

CS Fundamentals

Operating systems, networks and security. You print all three on your résumé, and Google asks them. These are the questions with objectively right answers, so they are free marks if you prepare and expensive if you do not.

3 modules · 16 concepts
//Operating Systems

Operating Systems

Processes, memory and synchronisation. Concurrency questions here are the same concepts you meet again in the GIL, in Java threads, and in your metering race conditions.

The line this defends

CS Fundamentals: Data Structures, Algorithms, System Design, Operating Systems, DBMS, Computer Networks

01

Process vs thread

Core

A process owns an address space; threads within it share that space. Sharing makes threads cheap to create and switch between, and makes them dangerous.

Think of it as

Separate offices versus desks in one room. Passing a note between desks is instant; it is also how two people end up editing the same page.

How it actually works
  • Process: own memory, file descriptors, PID. Isolated — a crash kills only that process. IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory) needed to communicate.
  • Thread: shares heap, code and file descriptors with its siblings; has its own stack, registers and program counter.
  • Context switch cost: thread switches are cheaper than process switches because the page tables and TLB do not change.
  • Shared state is the whole difficulty. Race conditions, deadlocks and torn reads all follow from shared mutable memory.
  • Coroutines / green threads are cheaper still — scheduled in user space, no kernel involvement. This is asyncio and Java's virtual threads.
02

Race conditions, mutexes & semaphores

On your résuméCore

A race condition is when the result depends on timing. A mutex allows exactly one holder; a semaphore allows N. The critical section is what you are protecting.

Think of it as

One toilet with one key versus a car park with N spaces. The mutex is ownership; the semaphore is counting.

How it actually works
  • Critical section: the code that must not run concurrently. Keep it as small as possible — long critical sections destroy throughput.
  • Mutex: binary, and has an owner — only the locker may unlock. Semaphore: a counter, no ownership, usable as a signal between threads.
  • Read-modify-write is the classic race. count++, or check-balance-then-deduct. This is exactly the billing concurrency problem.
  • Deadlock's four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption, circular wait. Break one — usually by imposing a global lock order.
  • Livelock: threads keep responding to each other and make no progress. Starvation: a thread never gets the lock.
  • Prefer lock-free primitives where possible — atomic compare-and-swap, or pushing the atomicity into the database or Redis, which is what you did.
Template
pythonThe same race, in three places you have met it
# In-process: read-modify-write is not atomic
with lock:                       # critical section as small as possible
    balance -= cost

# In the database: make the check and the write one statement
# UPDATE balances SET credits = credits - 1
#  WHERE tenant = 42 AND credits >= 1;      -- rowcount tells you if you won

# In Redis: Lua runs atomically on the single-threaded server
# if tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])) >= cost then
#     return redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], cost)
# end
# return -1

# Same bug, three layers. The fix is always: make check-and-act one
# indivisible operation, at whichever layer owns the truth.
They will ask

Break one of the four necessary conditions, and in practice the tractable one is circular wait: impose a global ordering on lock acquisition so every thread takes locks in the same sequence. If nobody can hold A and wait for B while someone holds B and waits for A, a cycle is impossible.

The other practical levers are lock timeouts — tryLock with a deadline so you back off and retry rather than hang — and reducing lock scope so the window is tiny. And where I can, avoiding locks entirely: an atomic compare-and-swap, or pushing the atomicity down to the database or Redis, which is what I did for credit deduction.

03

Virtual memory & paging

Core

Every process sees a private contiguous address space. The MMU translates virtual pages to physical frames, and pages not in RAM live on disk.

Think of it as

Everyone believes they have the whole warehouse. A clerk maps each requested aisle to wherever the goods actually are, fetching from off-site when needed.

How it actually works
  • Page fault: the page is not resident, so the kernel loads it from disk. A minor fault is cheap; a major fault hits disk and is thousands of times slower.
  • TLB caches recent translations. A TLB miss costs a page-table walk — this is why memory locality matters for performance.
  • Thrashing: the working set exceeds RAM, so the system spends its time paging rather than computing. Throughput collapses.
  • Swap makes a memory problem into a latency catastrophe. Many production systems disable swap for this reason — Kubernetes historically required it off.
  • Copy-on-write: fork() shares pages until one side writes. This is why forking a large process is cheap, and why Redis snapshots work the way they do.
04

Scheduling & context switching

Deep

The scheduler decides which runnable thread gets a core next. A context switch saves one thread's state and restores another's — cheap individually, expensive in bulk.

Think of it as

A receptionist juggling callers. Each swap costs a moment of remembering where you were; do it constantly and you get nothing done.

How it actually works
  • Pre-emptive — the kernel interrupts on a timer. Contrast with cooperative, where a task yields voluntarily (asyncio, and why one blocking call freezes the loop).
  • Linux CFS aims for fair CPU share weighted by nice value. Real-time classes exist for latency-critical work.
  • Context switch cost is roughly a microsecond of direct cost, plus a much larger indirect cost from cache and TLB pollution.
  • Load average counts runnable *plus* uninterruptible-sleep tasks on Linux — so high load with low CPU usually means I/O wait.
  • More threads is not more throughput. Past the core count for CPU-bound work, you add switching overhead and contention and go slower.
//Networking

Networking

TCP, TLS, HTTP and DNS. 'What happens when you type a URL' is still asked because it lets an interviewer probe any layer they choose.

01

TCP vs UDP

Core

TCP is a reliable ordered byte stream with a handshake, retransmission and congestion control. UDP is fire-and-forget datagrams with none of that.

Think of it as

Registered post with delivery confirmation versus dropping postcards in the box. One guarantees arrival and order; the other is faster and sometimes loses one.

How it actually works
  • TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) costs one round trip before any data flows. Over a long distance this dominates first-byte latency.
  • TCP gives: ordering, retransmission, flow control (receiver window) and congestion control (slow start, backoff).
  • UDP gives: low latency and no head-of-line blocking. Used for DNS, video, gaming, and as the base for QUIC.
  • Head-of-line blocking: one lost TCP segment stalls everything behind it, even data that already arrived. This is the flaw HTTP/3 and QUIC exist to fix.
  • Connection reuse matters enormously. Keep-alive and connection pools avoid paying the handshake per request — a common, large, easy win.
02

TLS handshake

Core

Asymmetric cryptography is used briefly to authenticate the server and agree a shared secret; everything after that is fast symmetric encryption.

Think of it as

Exchanging sealed introductions once, then switching to a shared codebook because it is far quicker to use.

How it actually works
  • TLS 1.3 needs one round trip (down from two in 1.2), and supports 0-RTT resumption for repeat connections.
  • The certificate proves identity — the server's public key signed by a CA your client trusts. This is what prevents man-in-the-middle.
  • Key exchange is ephemeral (ECDHE), giving forward secrecy: stealing the server's private key later does not decrypt past traffic.
  • Session resumption avoids a full handshake on reconnect, which matters for mobile clients on flaky networks.
  • mTLS additionally authenticates the client with its own certificate — common between services in a mesh, and in healthcare integrations.
03

HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3

Core

1.1 is one request at a time per connection. 2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection. 3 moves to QUIC over UDP to remove TCP head-of-line blocking.

Think of it as

One conversation per phone line; many conversations on one line; and finally many conversations that do not stall each other when one word is missed.

How it actually works
  • HTTP/1.1: keep-alive, but one outstanding request per connection — so browsers open six connections per host to fake parallelism.
  • HTTP/2: binary framing, stream multiplexing, header compression (HPACK), server push (largely abandoned). Still suffers TCP-level head-of-line blocking.
  • HTTP/3 / QUIC: streams are independent at the transport layer, so one lost packet stalls only its own stream. Also faster connection setup.
  • Practical impact: with HTTP/2, asset concatenation and domain sharding became counter-productive — old advice that is now wrong.
  • Idempotency and safety: GET/HEAD/OPTIONS are safe; GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent; POST is neither. Intermediaries rely on this.
04

What happens when you type a URL

Core

The classic. Answer it as layers, and let the interviewer pick which one to open up.

Think of it as

Posting a letter: find the address, plan the route, seal it, hand it over, wait for the reply, then read it.

How it actually works
  • 1. DNS resolution — browser cache → OS cache → resolver → root → TLD → authoritative. Returns an IP, with a TTL.
  • 2. TCP connection — three-way handshake to the IP on port 443 (or a reused pooled connection).
  • 3. TLS handshake — certificate validation, key agreement, then encrypted.
  • 4. HTTP request — method, path, headers, cookies. Likely hits a CDN edge first, then a load balancer, then your service.
  • 5. Server processing — gateway auth and rate limiting, application logic, database and cache reads, response assembly.
