  • 6. Response and render — parse HTML, build the DOM, fetch subresources, run CSS and JS, paint. Critical rendering path.
  • Say the layers first, then offer to go deep on any one. That structure is the signal being tested.
Say this

I'd break it into DNS, transport, TLS, the request path through CDN and load balancer to the app, then server processing and browser rendering. Which layer would you like me to go into?

05

REST, status codes & gRPC

Core

REST is resource-oriented HTTP with meaningful verbs and status codes. gRPC is binary RPC over HTTP/2 with a schema — faster and stricter, and worse for public APIs.

Think of it as

REST is a well-labelled public counter; gRPC is a direct intercom between two departments who agreed the phrasing in advance.

How it actually works
  • Status codes carry meaning: 200 ok, 201 created, 204 no content, 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 authenticated but forbidden, 404, 409 conflict, 422 validation, 429 rate limited, 500, 503.
  • 401 vs 403 is a standard filter — 401 means we do not know who you are, 403 means we do and you still may not.
  • Idempotency by verb: PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not, which is why it needs an idempotency key.
  • Pagination: cursor-based beats offset-based at scale — offset gets slower deeper into the results and skips rows when data shifts.
  • gRPC: protobuf schema, code generation, streaming both ways, much smaller payloads. Great service-to-service, awkward from a browser.
  • Versioning: put it in the path (/v1/) or a header. Whatever you choose, never break an existing contract in place.
They will ask

403 if they are authenticated and simply lack permission; 401 if they have not authenticated at all or the token is invalid.

But in a multi-tenant EHR I would often deliberately return 404 instead of 403 for cross-tenant access. A 403 confirms the resource exists, which leaks information — an attacker can enumerate valid claim IDs by watching for 403 versus 404. Returning 404 for anything outside your tenant scope means the response is identical whether or not the record exists.

06

CORS

Core

A browser-enforced rule that a page from one origin cannot read a response from another unless that server opts in with headers.

Think of it as

A doorman who lets you knock on any door but only lets you carry the reply home if that household put your name on a list.

How it actually works
  • It is browser-enforced only. CORS is not security for your API — a server-side client or curl ignores it entirely. Authorisation still has to be real.
  • Simple requests go straight out. Preflight (OPTIONS) happens for non-simple methods, custom headers or JSON content types.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin must echo a specific origin — not * — when credentials are involved, and Allow-Credentials: true is required for cookies.
  • The error is always on the browser side, which is why the server logs look clean and the developer is confused.
  • Same-origin means scheme, host and port all match. http vs https is a different origin.
//Security

Security

In a HIPAA product this is not a bonus round. Expect at least one security question, and your support-endpoint story is the answer to several of them.

01

Authentication vs authorisation

On your résuméCore

Authentication establishes who you are; authorisation decides what you may do. Conflating them is the root of most access-control bugs.

Think of it as

Showing your passport at the border versus what your visa lets you do once inside.

How it actually works
  • Authenticate at the edge, authorise in the service. The gateway can verify a token; only the domain knows whether this user may read this claim.
  • Deny by default. A new endpoint should be inaccessible until a rule grants access, not open until someone remembers to restrict it.
  • Authorise on every request, not once at login. A permission revoked mid-session must take effect.
  • Object-level authorisation is the one people miss — checking the role but not whether *this* user may see *this* record. It is the top item in the OWASP API list for a reason.
  • Never trust the client. Hiding a UI control is not a control; the endpoint must refuse.
02

Sessions vs JWT

Core

A session ID is a reference the server can look up and revoke. A JWT is a self-contained signed claim the server can verify without a lookup — and cannot easily un-issue.

Think of it as

A cloakroom ticket versus a signed letter of authority. The cloakroom can refuse a ticket instantly; the letter is valid until it expires.

How it actually works
  • Sessions: server-side state, instantly revocable, requires a shared store (Redis) to scale horizontally.
  • JWT: stateless, verifiable by signature, no lookup. Revocation is the hard problem — you need a denylist, which reintroduces the state you were avoiding.
  • Standard compromise: short-lived access token (5–15 min) plus a long-lived, revocable refresh token stored server-side.
  • Never put sensitive data in a JWT payload — it is base64, not encrypted. Anyone holding it can read it.
  • alg: none and algorithm confusion are classic JWT vulnerabilities. Pin the expected algorithm; never let the token choose it.
  • In a healthcare app, revocability matters. A compromised session for a clinician must be killable immediately, which pushes toward short expiry and server-side refresh.
They will ask

That depends entirely on the session design, and it is the reason I would not use long-lived stateless JWTs alone in a clinical product. With pure JWTs the token stays valid until it expires — you cannot un-issue it without a denylist, which means you have reintroduced server-side state anyway.

The design I would want is short-lived access tokens, five to fifteen minutes, with a revocable refresh token held server-side. Revoking the refresh token caps exposure at the access-token lifetime, which is a bounded and defensible window. And for genuinely immediate cut-off — which EPCS-scoped accounts warrant — a denylist checked at the gateway, accepting the lookup cost for that population.

03

OWASP: injection, XSS, CSRF

Core

The three classic web vulnerabilities. Each has one correct structural fix, and knowing the fix rather than the definition is what gets marked.

Think of it as

Three ways a forged instruction gets executed: smuggled into a command, into a page, or into a request the browser makes on your behalf.

How it actually works
  • SQL injection: untrusted input concatenated into a query. Fix: parameterised queries, always. Escaping is not a fix; an ORM is not automatically a fix if you use raw string interpolation.
  • XSS: untrusted input rendered as HTML or JS. Fix: context-aware output encoding plus a Content-Security-Policy. React escapes by default — dangerouslySetInnerHTML opts out.
  • CSRF: a third-party site causes the browser to send an authenticated request. Fix: SameSite=Lax cookies plus an anti-CSRF token on state-changing requests.
  • Stored vs reflected XSS: stored is worse — it persists and hits every viewer.
  • Prompt injection is the modern member of this family — untrusted text reaching an interpreter. Same shape, no escaping available, so the fix has to be at the tool boundary.
Template
pythonThe only correct fix for injection
# VULNERABLE — string interpolation into SQL
cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM claims WHERE id = '{claim_id}'")
# claim_id = "1' OR '1'='1"  ->  returns every claim in the table

# CORRECT — parameterised. The driver sends query and values separately,
# so the value can never be parsed as SQL.
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM claims WHERE id = %s AND tenant_id = %s",
            (claim_id, tenant_id))

# Still vulnerable through an ORM if you interpolate raw SQL:
# Claim.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM claims WHERE id = {claim_id}")  # NO
Claim.objects.filter(id=claim_id, tenant_id=tenant_id)              # yes
04

Hashing vs encryption vs encoding

Core

Encoding is reversible and not security (base64). Encryption is reversible with a key. Hashing is one-way. Using the wrong one is a common and serious mistake.

Think of it as

Translating a letter, locking it in a safe, or burning it and keeping the ash pattern. Only the last one cannot be undone.

How it actually works
  • Passwords are hashed, never encrypted — with a slow, salted, memory-hard function: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2. Never MD5, SHA-1 or plain SHA-256.
  • Salt is per-password and prevents rainbow tables. Work factor makes brute force expensive and should be raised as hardware improves.
  • Encryption for data you must read back — PHI at rest, API keys. AES-256-GCM gives confidentiality and integrity together.
  • Envelope encryption: a KMS master key wraps a per-tenant data key. This is the BYOK pattern you implemented.
  • Base64 is encoding, not encryption. A JWT payload and a Kubernetes Secret are both merely base64 — treat them as plaintext.
  • Never invent cryptography. Use a vetted library, and say so in the interview.
05

Secrets management

On your résuméCore

Credentials never live in code, in an image layer, in a log, or in an environment variable committed to a repo. They come from a secret store at runtime and rotate.

Think of it as

Keys collected from a keybox on arrival, not taped under the doormat where the previous tenant also knew to look.

How it actually works
  • Use a real store: AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, or cloud-native workload identity. Injected at runtime, never baked into the artefact.
  • Prefer short-lived credentials — an IAM role or workload identity gives rotating tokens, removing the long-lived key entirely.
  • Rotation must be routine, not an incident response. If rotating is scary, that itself is the finding.
  • Scan for secrets in CI and pre-commit. People will commit keys; the question is whether you find out in minutes or months.
  • Docker image layers are immutable and shipped — a secret added and then deleted is still in the image history.
  • On leak: rotate first, then clean history. Cleaning without rotating achieves nothing.
06

Threat modelling in one minute

Deep

A structured way to answer 'is this design secure'. Ask: what are we protecting, who wants it, how would they get it, and what stops them.

Think of it as

Walking around a building asking where you would break in, rather than checking the front door is locked and declaring victory.

How it actually works
  • Assets: PHI, credentials, model keys, audit logs. Name what actually matters rather than everything equally.
  • Actors: external attacker, malicious insider, a compromised third party, and an honest user making a mistake.
  • STRIDE as a checklist: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
  • Trust boundaries are where the interesting bugs live — between browser and server, between service and third party, between agent and tool.
  • Mitigate structurally, not procedurally. 'We are careful' is not a control; 'the projection cannot contain PHI' is.
  • This framing is exactly how you would present the support-endpoint design in an interview.
Say this

The question I asked was what could travel down this new path that should not. PHI was the asset, a compromised support account was the actor, and the mitigation had to be structural — an explicit projection rather than entity serialisation — because 'we'll be careful with the fields' is not a control.

/DSA Interview Layer

DSA Interview Layer

Not a replacement for the 30-day program in the DSA Lab — this is the layer on top: how to run the 45 minutes, which pattern the trigger words point to, and the Python templates worth having in muscle memory.

5 modules · 16 concepts
//Running the Coding Round

Running the Coding Round

Google scores communication and problem-solving as separate signals from correctness. Two candidates with identical working code get different scores, and this module is why.

01

The seven-step protocol

Core

Clarify → examples → brute force → optimise → confirm → code → test. Never start typing at minute one, and never stay silent.

Think of it as

A pilot's checklist. Not because you would forget the plane needs fuel, but because under pressure people skip exactly the step that matters.

How it actually works
  • 1. Clarify (2 min): input types, size bounds, duplicates, negatives, empty input, sorted or not, is the input mutable, what to return on no-answer.
  • 2. Examples (1 min): work one small case by hand. This catches misunderstanding before it costs you twenty minutes.
  • 3. Brute force (2 min): state it and its complexity out loud. Never skip it — it proves you understand the problem and gives you a correctness baseline.
  • 4. Optimise (5 min): what is the repeated work? Name the pattern. Say the target complexity before you write it.
  • 5. Confirm: "I'm going to use a hash map for O(n) time, O(n) space — shall I code that?" Interviewers will redirect you here if you are wrong.
  • 6. Code (15 min): narrate as you go. Clean names, small helpers, no cleverness.
  • 7. Test (5 min): walk a real example line by line, then the edge cases you listed in step 1.
Trap

Jumping straight to the optimal solution in silence. Even if it is right, you have shown none of the problem-solving signal the round exists to measure — and if it is wrong, you have nothing to fall back on.

02

Thinking out loud

Core

Your reasoning is the product, not your code. An interviewer cannot give credit for thinking they did not hear.

Think of it as

Showing your working in an exam. The final number earns some marks; the method earns most of them.

How it actually works
  • Narrate the search, not just the answer: "Sorting would let me two-pointer this, but that's O(n log n) — a hash map gets me O(n) if I can trade space."
  • Say why you rejected things. Rejecting an approach for a stated reason is a positive signal.
  • When stuck, say what you are stuck on. Silence reads as being lost; "I'm trying to find a way to avoid recomputing this subarray sum" invites a hint you can be given credit for using.
  • Take the hint gracefully. Interviewers expect to nudge. Fighting a hint is far worse than taking it.
  • Do not narrate syntax. "Now I'm writing a for loop" is noise. Narrate decisions, not keystrokes.
Say this

Let me restate the problem to make sure I have it, then I'll walk a small example, give you the brute force with its complexity, and then talk through how I'd improve it before I write anything.

03

The clarifying questions that always pay

Core

A short fixed list you can run on any problem. It takes ninety seconds and prevents the single most expensive failure — solving the wrong problem.

Think of it as

Measuring twice. The cut takes the same time either way.

How it actually works
  • Size: how large can n be? This tells you the target complexity — n ≤ 20 hints at exponential/bitmask, n ≤ 10⁵ at O(n log n), n ≤ 10⁹ at O(log n) or maths.
  • Contents: negatives? duplicates? empty? already sorted? all one type?
  • Output: return the value or the index? All answers or any one? What if there is no answer — null, empty, or an exception?
  • Constraints: may I mutate the input? Is extra space allowed? Is it a stream or all in memory?
  • Ambiguity: for anything string-related, ask about case sensitivity, whitespace and unicode.
  • Then state your assumptions explicitly and move on. Do not spend five minutes here.
//Complexity

Complexity

You must be able to state and justify the complexity of anything you write, instantly and correctly. This is a hard filter.

01

Big-O, and what it actually measures

Core

An upper bound on growth as input size increases, ignoring constants. It tells you how the cost scales, not how fast the code runs.

Think of it as

Describing a road as uphill rather than giving the gradient. It tells you what happens over distance, not your speed today.

How it actually works
  • The ladder: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!).
  • Constants are dropped but matter in practice. An O(n) pass with a huge constant can lose to O(n log n) at realistic sizes — say this when it is relevant.
  • Analyse the dominant term. Two sequential loops are O(n); nested loops are O(n²).
  • Recursion: cost = number of nodes in the call tree × work per node. Fibonacci naively is O(2ⁿ) because the tree branches twice at every level.
  • Space complexity includes the call stack. A recursive tree traversal is O(h) space even with no explicit data structure — this is frequently forgotten.
  • Amortised is average-per-operation over a sequence. list.append is amortised O(1): occasional O(n) resizes spread over many cheap appends.
Template
pythonState the complexity of every branch, including the stack
# O(n) time, O(n) space — the hash map is the space cost
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                      # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:     # O(1) average lookup
            return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []

# O(n) time, O(h) space — h = tree height. The call stack IS space.
# Balanced: O(log n). Degenerate (a linked list): O(n).
def depth(node):
    if not node:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(depth(node.left), depth(node.right))
They will ask

O(h), where h is the height of the tree — the call stack holds one frame per level on the current path, even though the code allocates nothing explicitly. That is the part people miss.

For a balanced tree that is O(log n); for a degenerate tree that has become a linked list it is O(n), which is also where you get a stack overflow in practice. If you needed guaranteed O(1) extra space, Morris traversal achieves it by temporarily rewiring right pointers, at the cost of mutating the tree during the walk.

02

Reading the constraints

Core

The stated input bounds tell you the intended complexity. Use them — it converts an open search into a narrow one.

Think of it as

A recipe that says it serves four tells you the pan size before you start cooking.

How it actually works
  • n ≤ 12 → permutations, O(n!). n ≤ 20 → subsets or bitmask DP, O(2ⁿ).
  • n ≤ 2,000 → O(n²) is fine. Two nested loops, or 2-D DP.
  • n ≤ 10⁵ or 10⁶ → O(n log n) or O(n). Sorting, heap, two pointers, sliding window, hash map.
  • n ≤ 10⁹ → O(log n) or O(1). Binary search on the answer, or maths.
  • Roughly 10⁸ simple operations per second is the usual budget. Multiply your complexity by n and sanity-check it.
  • Say this out loud: "n is up to 10⁵, so I'm aiming for O(n log n) at worst." It shows you read the problem properly.
//Pattern Triggers

Pattern Triggers

The lookup table that converts problem wording into an approach. Read this the morning of a coding round.

01

Trigger → pattern map

Core

Most interview problems announce their pattern in the wording. Learn the mapping and you skip most of the search.

Think of it as

Symptoms to diagnosis. You still examine the patient, but you know which three things to check first.

How it actually works
  • "sorted array" + pair/triplet → two pointers from the ends. "find target in sorted" → binary search.
  • "contiguous subarray/substring" + constraint → sliding window. "subarray sum equals k" → prefix sum + hash map.
  • "top k" / "k largest" / "k closest" → heap of size k, O(n log k).
  • "next greater/smaller element" → monotonic stack. "valid parentheses" / nesting → stack.
  • "shortest path, unweighted" → BFS. "all paths" / "connected components" / "islands" → DFS. "weighted shortest path" → Dijkstra.
  • "prerequisites" / "ordering" / "dependency" → topological sort. "cycle in a directed graph" → DFS with three colours.
  • "max/min" or "how many ways" with overlapping subproblems → dynamic programming. "all combinations/permutations" → backtracking.
  • "merge intervals" / "overlapping" → sort by start, then sweep. "detect cycle in linked list" → fast and slow pointers.
  • "prefix" / "autocomplete" / "dictionary" → trie. "connected groups with union" → union-find.
  • "minimise the maximum" or "maximise the minimum" → binary search on the answer. This one is high-value and frequently missed.
02

Binary search on the answer

Deep

When the answer is a number in a range and you can cheaply check 'is X feasible', binary search the answer space rather than an array.

Think of it as

Guessing a price with hot-or-cold feedback. You never enumerate every price; you halve the range each guess.

How it actually works
  • The trigger phrases: "minimise the maximum", "maximise the minimum", "smallest capacity such that...", "least time to complete".
  • Requirement: monotonicity. If X works, everything above X works (or below, depending on direction). Say this out loud — it is what justifies the approach.
  • Write the feasibility check first as a separate function. It is usually a simple greedy pass, and separating it makes the binary search trivial.
  • Complexity is O(n log(range)) — the log is over the value range, not the array length.
  • Classic problems: ship packages within D days, split array largest sum, koko eating bananas, minimum time to make bouquets.
Template
pythonThe shape — feasibility function, then search the range
def min_capacity(weights, days):
    # Feasibility: can we finish within `days` at this capacity?
    # Monotonic: if cap works, cap+1 works. That is what licenses
    # binary search over the ANSWER instead of over an array.
    def feasible(cap):
        need, cur = 1, 0
        for w in weights:
            if cur + w > cap:
                need += 1
                cur = 0
            cur += w
        return need <= days

    lo = max(weights)          # must fit the heaviest single item
    hi = sum(weights)          # everything in one day always works
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if feasible(mid):
            hi = mid           # keep mid: it might be the answer
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo
//Python Templates

Python Templates

The dozen shapes that cover most of what you will be asked. Type them from memory until the boilerplate costs no thought.

01

Binary search — the bounds that never go wrong

Core

Use the half-open lo < hi form. It eliminates the off-by-one and the infinite-loop bugs that cost people whole interviews.

Think of it as

A ruler marked at the edges rather than the middle of each unit. The arithmetic stops being ambiguous.

How it actually works
  • while lo < hi with hi = mid and lo = mid + 1 cannot infinite-loop, because mid is always strictly less than hi.
  • bisect_left / bisect_right from the standard library handle sorted-array insertion directly. Use them when allowed.
  • Rotated sorted array: one half is always sorted — determine which by comparing nums[lo] to nums[mid], then decide which half contains the target.
  • Say the invariant out loud: "the answer is always in [lo, hi)". That is what makes the bounds obviously correct.
Template
pythonThree variants, one safe shape
# Leftmost index where target could be inserted (== bisect_left)
def lower_bound(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)                  # half-open [lo, hi)
    while lo < hi:                      # invariant: answer in [lo, hi)
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid                    # mid may be the answer, keep it
    return lo

# Rotated sorted array: one side is always sorted
def search_rotated(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target: return mid
        if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:                 # left half sorted
            if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]: hi = mid - 1
            else:                              lo = mid + 1
        else:                                     # right half sorted
            if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1
            else:                              hi = mid - 1
    return -1
02

Sliding window

Core

Expand the right edge always; shrink the left edge while the window is invalid. Every element enters and leaves once, so it is O(n).

Think of it as

A caterpillar. The head moves forward continuously; the tail catches up only when it has to.

How it actually works
  • Variable window: grow right, shrink left while a constraint is violated. For longest/shortest-subarray problems.
  • Fixed window: move both edges together, adding the entering element and removing the leaving one.
  • The state is usually a counter or a hash map of what is currently inside the window.
  • Say the invariant: "the window [l, r] is always valid after the inner while loop" — that is the proof of correctness.
  • Monotonic deque variant for sliding window maximum, which keeps it O(n) instead of O(n·k).
Template
pythonThe one shape that covers both directions
from collections import Counter, deque

# Longest substring with at most k distinct characters
def longest_k_distinct(s, k):
    count, left, best = Counter(), 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        count[ch] += 1
        while len(count) > k:              # shrink until valid again
            count[s[left]] -= 1
            if count[s[left]] == 0:
                del count[s[left]]         # keep len(count) honest
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1) # window is valid here
    return best

# Sliding window maximum in O(n) with a monotonic deque of INDICES
def max_window(nums, k):
    dq, out = deque(), []
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        while dq and nums[dq[-1]] <= x: dq.pop()      # keep decreasing
        dq.append(i)
        if dq[0] <= i - k: dq.popleft()               # drop out-of-window
        if i >= k - 1: out.append(nums[dq[0]])
    return out
03

BFS, DFS & topological sort

Core

BFS with a deque for shortest path in an unweighted graph. DFS recursive or with a stack for reachability and components. Kahn's algorithm for ordering.

Think of it as

BFS is a ripple spreading evenly; DFS is one explorer going as deep as possible before backtracking.

How it actually works
  • BFS gives shortest path in unweighted graphs because it visits in order of distance. DFS does not.
  • Mark visited when you enqueue, not when you dequeue — otherwise a node can be added many times before it is processed.
  • Level-order: capture len(queue) at the top of the loop to process one level at a time.
  • Grid problems are graphs — neighbours are the four (or eight) adjacent cells with bounds checks.
  • Topological sort (Kahn's): repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree zero. If you cannot empty the graph, there is a cycle — which is also how you detect one.
  • Cycle detection in a directed graph with DFS needs three states (unvisited, in-progress, done), not a boolean.
Template
pythonThe three graph traversals you will actually need
from collections import deque, defaultdict

def bfs_shortest(graph, start, goal):
    q, seen = deque([(start, 0)]), {start}      # mark on ENQUEUE
    while q:
        node, d = q.popleft()
        if node == goal: return d
        for nb in graph[node]:
            if nb not in seen:
                seen.add(nb)
                q.append((nb, d + 1))
    return -1

def topo_sort(n, edges):
    graph, indeg = defaultdict(list), [0] * n
    for u, v in edges:                          # u must come before v
        graph[u].append(v); indeg[v] += 1

    q = deque([i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0])
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft(); order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0: q.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else []     # short == cycle exists

# Grid DFS: neighbours are the 4 adjacent cells
DIRS = ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1))
04

Dynamic programming

Core

Define the state, write the transition, set the base case. Top-down memoisation is easier to derive; bottom-up is easier to space-optimise.

Think of it as

Building a wall from the bottom. Each row rests on the one below, and you never re-lay a row you already have.

How it actually works
  • Say the state out loud first: "dp[i] is the best answer considering the first i items." Getting the state right is 80% of the problem.
  • Top-down = recursion + @cache. Fastest to write in an interview and the transition mirrors the recurrence directly.
  • Bottom-up = fill a table in dependency order. Necessary when you want to reduce the space.
  • Space optimisation: if dp[i] only depends on dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], keep two variables instead of an array.
  • The families worth knowing: 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, longest increasing subsequence, coin change, house robber, edit distance, and interval DP.
  • When stuck, write the brute-force recursion first, then add @cache. That converts exponential to polynomial almost for free.
Template
pythonSame problem three ways — derive, tabulate, compress
from functools import cache

# 1. Top-down: write the recurrence, add one decorator.
@cache
def rob(i, houses):
    if i < 0: return 0
    return max(rob(i - 1, houses),                    # skip
               rob(i - 2, houses) + houses[i])        # take

# 2. Bottom-up: same recurrence, filled in dependency order.
def rob_table(houses):
    n = len(houses)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    dp[1] = houses[0] if n else 0
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + houses[i - 1])
    return dp[n]

# 3. Space-optimised: dp[i] only needs the last two values.
def rob_opt(houses):
    prev2 = prev1 = 0
    for x in houses:
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, max(prev1, prev2 + x)
    return prev1                                      # O(1) space
05

Backtracking

Core

Choose, recurse, un-choose. One shape generates permutations, combinations, subsets, N-queens and sudoku.

Think of it as

Exploring a maze with chalk. Mark the path, go on, and rub out the mark when you come back so the next attempt is unaffected.

How it actually works
  • The invariant: the state must be identical before and after each recursive call returns. The un-choose step is what guarantees it.
  • Append a copy (path[:]) when recording a result, or every entry aliases the same list and you end up with a list of empty lists.
  • Pruning is where the performance is — sort first, then skip branches that cannot lead to a valid answer.
  • Duplicate handling: sort the input and skip i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1] to avoid emitting the same combination twice.
  • Complexity: roughly the number of nodes in the search tree times the work per node — usually O(n · 2ⁿ) or O(n · n!). State it honestly.
Template
pythonOne shape, three problems
def subsets(nums):
    out, path = [], []
    def bt(start):
        out.append(path[:])                # COPY, not a reference
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])           # choose
            bt(i + 1)                      # recurse
            path.pop()                     # UN-choose: restore state
    bt(0)
    return out

def combination_sum(candidates, target):
    candidates.sort()                      # enables the prune below
    out, path = [], []
    def bt(start, remaining):
        if remaining == 0:
            out.append(path[:]); return
        for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
            if candidates[i] > remaining:
                break                      # sorted: nothing later fits
            if i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i - 1]:
                continue                   # skip duplicate branches
            path.append(candidates[i])
            bt(i + 1, remaining - candidates[i])
            path.pop()
    bt(0, target)
    return out
06

Heaps, tries & union-find

Core

The three data structures whose absence turns an elegant solution into a quadratic one.

Think of it as

A priority queue at triage, an index by prefix, and a way to ask instantly whether two people are already in the same group.

How it actually works
  • Heap: heapq is a min-heap on a list. For top-k, keep a heap of size k and evict — O(n log k), not O(n log n).
  • Max-heap in Python: push -value, or push tuples (-priority, item).
  • Trie: a tree keyed by character, for prefix queries and autocomplete. O(length of word) lookup, independent of dictionary size.
  • Union-find (disjoint set): near-O(1) with path compression and union by rank. For connectivity, cycle detection in undirected graphs, and Kruskal's MST.
  • Recognise union-find from the wording: "are these connected", "number of groups", "redundant connection".
Template
pythonUnion-find with both optimisations, in ten lines
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank = [0] * n

    def find(self, x):
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]  # path compression
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a, b):
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False                     # already connected -> a cycle
        if self.rank[ra] < self.rank[rb]:    # union by rank keeps it flat
            ra, rb = rb, ra
        self.parent[rb] = ra
        if self.rank[ra] == self.rank[rb]:
            self.rank[ra] += 1
        return True

# Top-k with a bounded heap: O(n log k)
import heapq
def top_k(nums, k):
    h = []
    for x in nums:
        heapq.heappush(h, x)
        if len(h) > k: heapq.heappop(h)      # evict the smallest
    return h
//Edge Cases & Testing

Edge Cases & Testing

The last five minutes, where a lot of otherwise-passing interviews are lost.

01

The edge-case checklist

Core

A fixed list to run against any solution before you say you are done. Finding your own bug scores better than the interviewer finding it.

Think of it as

Pre-flight checks. Boring, fast, and the reason planes rarely fall out of the sky.

How it actually works
  • Empty input — empty list, empty string, null root. The single most common miss.
  • One element, and two elements. Many two-pointer and window solutions break at n = 1.
  • All identical values, and all distinct.
  • Negatives and zero — especially in sums, products and division.
  • Overflow — not in Python, but say it if the interviewer is thinking in Java or C++.
  • Already sorted, and reverse sorted — the worst case for naive quicksort and for many greedy approaches.
  • Cycles in a graph or linked list, and disconnected components.
  • Boundaries: first and last index, and the exact threshold value in any comparison.
Say this

Let me walk through the edge cases before I call this done: empty input, a single element, all duplicates, and negatives. [Then actually trace each one.]

02

Trace, do not skim

Core

Walk a real example line by line with actual values, out loud. Skimming your own code finds nothing, because you read what you meant to write.

Think of it as

Proofreading your own essay. You see the intended sentence, not the one on the page — until you read it aloud.

How it actually works
  • Write the variable values down as you step through. Do not hold them in your head.
  • Trace a case with at least three elements — one and two-element cases hide off-by-one errors rather than exposing them.
  • Check loop boundaries specifically: does the last element get processed? Does the first?
  • If you find a bug, say so and fix it calmly. Finding your own bug is a strong positive signal, not a failure.
  • Then state the complexity again, in both time and space, as your closing line.
03

When you are completely stuck

Core

A recovery procedure. Being stuck is normal and survivable; being stuck silently is not.

Think of it as

A climber who has lost the route. The move is to call it in, not to keep quietly grasping at the rock.

How it actually works
  • Say it explicitly and specifically: "I'm stuck on how to avoid recomputing the sum for each window." That is a question an interviewer can answer.
  • Go back to brute force and code it. A working O(n²) beats a broken O(n). You can then optimise from something that runs.
  • Try a smaller case by hand. Solve n = 3 on paper; the pattern often falls out.
  • Reach for the trigger list: what does the problem structure resemble? Sorted? Nested? Overlapping subproblems?
  • Ask for a hint if you have been stuck for two minutes. Interviewers expect it, it costs less than you think, and using a hint well is itself a positive signal.
Trap

Silent flailing for ten minutes. It converts a recoverable round into an unrecoverable one, because you have produced neither code nor visible reasoning.

/The Loop & The Plan

The Loop & The Plan

The rounds you will actually sit, the story bank to sit them with, and a dated plan from today to an offer. Written for the Google L4 target specifically.

4 modules · 20 concepts
//What Each Round Measures

What Each Round Measures

Google scores four attributes independently, and each round is a probe into one or more of them. Knowing which one you are being measured on changes how you answer.

01

The four scoring attributes

Core

General Cognitive Ability, Role-Related Knowledge, Leadership, and Googleyness. Every interviewer submits scores against these, and a hiring committee reads the packet — not the interviewers' overall impressions.

Think of it as

A driving test scored on four separate sheets. Being brilliant at parallel parking does not offset failing to check mirrors.

How it actually works
  • GCA — how you approach an ambiguous problem. Measured mostly in the coding and design rounds, and it is about *process*, not just the answer.
  • RRK — do you know the craft. Your résumé depth, system design, and language fundamentals.
  • Leadership — emergent leadership, not management. Influencing without authority, stepping up, driving something nobody assigned.
  • Googleyness — ambiguity tolerance, bias to action, collaboration, intellectual humility, doing the right thing.
  • The packet is written, so the interviewer is taking notes to justify a score. Give them quotable, specific evidence.
  • A hiring committee that never met you decides. That is why vague answers fail — they do not survive being written down.
02

The L4 loop shape

Core

Typically a recruiter screen, one phone/virtual technical screen, then an onsite of four to five rounds: two to three coding, often one design, and one Googleyness & Leadership.

Think of it as

A qualifying lap followed by the race. The screen only decides whether you start.

How it actually works
  • Recruiter screen: logistics, level calibration, and your 90-second intro. Have your YOE, title and target level straight — this is where levelling is set.
  • Technical screen (45 min): one or two coding problems, usually medium. Python is your language; say so up front.
  • Onsite coding rounds: medium to medium-hard, 45 minutes each, usually two problems or one with follow-ups. Communication is scored, not just correctness.
  • Design round: at L4 this is often present but weighted less than at L5. Structure and trade-off articulation matter more than exotic components.
  • Googleyness & Leadership: behavioural, STAR format, roughly five to six questions in 45 minutes. Prepared and specific beats spontaneous and vague every time.
  • Team match comes after the loop passes and is the unpredictable tail — this is why the realistic offer date is Jan–Feb 2027, not December.
Trap

Treating the behavioural round as the easy one. It is the round most commonly under-prepared, and a weak Leadership or Googleyness score sinks packets with strong coding.

03

STAR, done properly

Core

Situation, Task, Action, Result — with roughly 70% of your words in Action, and the Result quantified. Most people invert this and spend three minutes on context.

Think of it as

A news report. Headline and outcome up front, then what was actually done. Nobody buries the story in paragraph nine.

How it actually works
  • Situation (15%): two sentences of context. Not the company history.
  • Task (10%): what specifically was *yours*. Be precise about the boundary of your ownership.
  • Action (60%): what *you* did, decision by decision, including the trade-offs you weighed and what you rejected. Say "I", not "we".
  • Result (15%): quantified, plus what you learned or would do differently. The reflection is where senior signal lives.
  • Two to three minutes total. Time yourself out loud — written and spoken length differ enormously.
  • "We" is the most common failure. Interviewers cannot score a team. Credit the team once, then speak in first person.
Say this

I'll give you the context quickly and then spend most of the time on what I actually did and why — stop me if you want more background.

//Your Story Bank

Your Story Bank

Eight stories drawn from your résumé, mapped to the questions they answer. Rehearse these out loud until each runs to two and a half minutes without notes.

01

Story 1 — The provisioning CLI (initiative)

On your résuméCore

Your best Leadership story, because nobody assigned it, you quantified it before building, and it changed how 40 engineers work.

Think of it as

The strongest evidence is always the work that would not exist if you had not decided it should.

How it actually works
  • Answers: "tell me about something you did that nobody asked for", "a time you improved a process", "how do you handle inefficiency", "influencing without authority".
  • S: New engineers were losing 1–2 days to environment setup, pulling in 3–4 existing engineers each time.
  • T: Nobody owned this. I decided to, alongside my normal work.
  • A: Quantified the cost first. Built a 12-phase idempotent provisioner where each phase checks, applies and independently verifies — so a failed run resumes rather than restarting. Then made the key decision: packaged it as a versioned CLI rather than a script, so build-process changes ship as a version bump.
  • R: 1–2 days and 3–4 engineers became a single 10-minute command, adopted by all 40 engineers across India and the US.
  • Reflection: the setup time was the visible win; the durable one was creating a distribution channel for build changes that previously travelled by Slack message.
Say this

Nobody asked me to build this. I'd watched three new joiners each lose two days to environment setup while pulling in senior engineers to unblock them, so I did the arithmetic first — and it was clearly worth a week of my time.

02

Story 2 — The Copilot rebuild (technical depth)

On your résuméCore

Your best Role-Related Knowledge story. It has a forcing function, a measured before and after, a mechanism, and a risk mitigation.

Think of it as

The full arc: why it had to change, what you changed, how you knew it worked, and what you did in case it did not.

How it actually works
  • Answers: "most technically challenging project", "a time you had to make a risky change", "how do you approach performance work".
  • S: Charm Copilot ran on OpenAI's Assistants API, which was being deprecated. Responses took 8–15 seconds.
  • T: I owned rebuilding the backend without regressing a clinical feature in production.
  • A: Profiled first and found the model was not the bottleneck — polling dead-time, a server-side thread refetch per turn, and serialised tool calls were. Built an in-house agentic runtime: conversation state in Redis, an owned tool loop with parallel execution and per-tool timeouts, and token streaming. Then the risk decision: shipped both runtimes in the same binary behind a per-tenant flag defaulting to the old path.
  • R: 8–15 seconds down to 2–5, with time-to-first-token sub-second. Rollback became a config flip rather than a 4–5 day hotfix.
  • Reflection: the flag cost real complexity — every bug reproduced twice — and it was still the right call for a clinical feature.
Trap

Have p50 and p95 for both runtimes ready. "8–15 seconds" is a range, and the follow-up is always "was that median or tail?"

03

Story 3 — The per-token switch (judgement)

On your résuméCore

Your best judgement story: you modelled a problem nobody had noticed, found a real risk, and shipped the mitigation off by default.

Think of it as

Fitting the sprinkler before the fire, and not turning it on.

How it actually works
  • Answers: "a decision you made with incomplete information", "a time you thought beyond your immediate task", "how do you balance business and engineering concerns".
  • S: Copilot was priced as a flat $75 per provider per month.
  • T: I was building the subscription layer. Modelling the unit economics was not part of it.
  • A: Ran cost per practice against the flat fee and found the tail — usage is heavy-tailed, and high-volume practices crossed into negative margin. Considered fair-use caps, throttling and volume tiers; each damaged the majority to fix a minority. Built a per-token switch instead, per-tenant, off by default.
  • R: The lever existed before it was needed, with no change to anyone's pricing and no time pressure.
  • Reflection: the engineering was small; the value was optionality. I would now want a dashboard tracking margin per tenant so it is monitored, not modelled once.
Say this

Nobody asked me to model this. I was building the metering and it seemed worth checking whether the pricing model held at the tail — it didn't, for a small number of heavy practices.

04

Story 4 — Support endpoints (influence & security)

On your résuméCore

Influencing without authority, through a security review, across two timezones — and the result became a team pattern.

Think of it as

Changing the building code rather than getting one house approved.

How it actually works
  • Answers: "influencing without authority", "handling disagreement", "a time you improved things for other people", "a security decision you made".
  • S: Support agents escalated to engineers for anything they could not see, consuming a large share of developer time.
  • T: I proposed exposing read-only diagnostic endpoints — in a HIPAA product, a genuinely contentious idea.
  • A: Reviewers were rightly sceptical of any new read path to production data. What resolved it was changing the shape of the proposal: from 'these endpoints are safe' to 'PHI cannot travel this path by construction' — explicit projection records rather than serialised entities, enforcement in the shared API security layer rather than per-endpoint, read-only, fully audited. Took it through a joint India–US review.
  • R: 60–80% of that escalation load removed, and the pattern was adopted team-wide.
  • Reflection: the objection dissolved when the guarantee became structural instead of a promise to be careful.
05

Story 5 — The e-KYC threshold (trade-offs)

On your résuméCore

A decision with no correct answer, only a trade-off you had to own: fraud caught versus real doctors locked out.

Think of it as

Setting the sensitivity on a smoke alarm in a kitchen.

How it actually works
  • Answers: "a difficult trade-off", "a decision with no right answer", "how do you handle ambiguity", "a time you disagreed on requirements".
  • S: Fraudulent accounts, and an EPCS regulatory requirement for identity proofing.
  • T: I built the platform across six flows — and had to choose the face-match threshold.
  • A: Framed it as false accept versus false reject. A false accept is a fraudulent account with prescribing capability; a false reject is a real physician blocked at signup. With EPCS in scope the asymmetry favoured strictness — but past a point you reject legitimate users for lighting and camera quality. So I set it high and built a manual review queue for the band just below, converting false rejects into a slower path rather than a lost user.
  • R: 67% reduction in fraudulent accounts, 60,000+ users onboarded.
  • Reflection: the review queue is what made the strict threshold defensible. Without it, the same number would have meant locking out real doctors.
Trap

Know your measurement methodology for the 67% — denominator, window, and the honest caveat that some of the drop is deterrence rather than detection.

06

Story 6 — A failure you own

Core

You will be asked. Have a real one with genuine cost, real ownership, and a systemic fix — not a humblebrag.

Think of it as

A scar, not a beauty mark. Interviewers can tell the difference immediately.

How it actually works
  • Answers: "tell me about a failure", "a time you were wrong", "your biggest mistake", "a time you received difficult feedback".
  • Choose one with real consequence — an outage, a wrong technical call, a rollout that hurt users, a deadline you missed.
  • Own it in first person. "I misjudged", not "the requirements were unclear". Blaming circumstances is the failure mode of this question.
  • The fix must be systemic, not "I'll be more careful". A test, a guardrail, a review step, a monitor.
  • Show the learning was durable — point at something you have done differently since.
  • Never use a fake weakness. "I work too hard" reads as evasion and costs you the Googleyness score directly.
Say this

The honest version is that I under-tested a path I assumed was covered. What I changed wasn't 'be more careful' — I added the check to CI so the same class of mistake fails the build rather than reaching production.

07

Story 7 — Cross-team & cross-timezone

Core

India–US collaboration is directly on your résumé and directly relevant to Google India, where most teams work across timezones.

Think of it as

Playing in an orchestra where half the section is on a five-hour delay. The score has to be written down.

How it actually works
  • Answers: "working with a distributed team", "a communication challenge", "how do you handle a disagreement with someone senior".
  • The specifics that matter: written proposals rather than meetings, decisions that survive without you in the room, and async review as the default.
  • Use the joint India–US security review, and the 40-engineer CLI rollout across two countries.
  • Name the concrete adaptations: overlapping-hours discipline, documenting decisions and their rationale, and making the artefact readable without you narrating it.
  • Google cares about this because most India-based teams have US stakeholders. It is a directly relevant, verifiable strength.
08

Story 8 — Why Google, why now

Core

Asked in nearly every loop and in the recruiter screen. A generic answer is a wasted opportunity; a specific one is memorable.

Think of it as

A proposal, not a job application. Say something true about them, not something flattering about anyone.

How it actually works
  • Be specific about scale: you have built AI systems for 10,000+ practices under a strict regulatory constraint. The honest pull is systems where scale itself is the hard problem.
  • Be specific about craft: you have been the person defining engineering standards on a small team. You want to be somewhere those standards are already high and you learn from them.
  • Do not criticise your current employer. Frame as moving toward, never away.
  • "Why now" has a real answer: four years of depth in one product and one domain, and you want the next problem to be different in kind, not just in size.
  • Avoid the clichés: 'impact at scale' and 'solving hard problems' without a specific referent are noise.
Say this

I've spent four years going deep on one product — AI systems inside a regulated EHR, where the constraint has always been compliance rather than scale. I want the next hard problem to be one where the scale itself is the constraint, and I want to be somewhere the engineering bar is set by people ahead of me rather than by me.

//Googleyness & Leadership

Googleyness & Leadership

The round most people under-prepare. These are the actual question shapes, and what each is really probing.

01

The questions and what they are really asking

Core

Every behavioural question maps to one of a handful of underlying attributes. Recognise the attribute and you know which story to reach for.

Think of it as

A menu with eight dishes and three actual ingredients. Learn the ingredients and you can cook anything on it.

How it actually works
  • "Ambiguous problem with no clear owner" → bias to action + comfort with ambiguity. Use the provisioning CLI.
  • "Disagreed with a decision" → intellectual humility + backbone. They want you to have disagreed, been heard, and either changed minds *or* committed anyway.
  • "Influenced without authority" → emergent leadership. Use the support endpoints and the joint review.
  • "Made a decision with incomplete data" → judgement. Use the per-token switch.
  • "Something failed" → ownership and learning. Use your real failure, systemically fixed.
  • "Handled a difficult teammate" → collaboration. Focus on what you did, never on their faults.
  • "Had to learn something quickly" → learning agility. The agentic rebuild works — Assistants API deprecating, and you rebuilt on your own runtime.
02

Intellectual humility

Core

Google explicitly screens for it. The signal is being able to say "I was wrong and here is what changed my mind" without it costing you anything.

Think of it as

A scientist who updates on evidence, versus a lawyer who defends the position they started with.

How it actually works
  • Have a specific example of changing your mind based on someone else's argument — ideally someone more junior than you.
  • Acknowledge the limits of your own numbers. Volunteering that $10M is projected, not booked, is intellectual humility demonstrated rather than claimed.
  • When you do not know something, say so cleanly and then say how you would find out. Bluffing is the single fastest way to lose a technical round.
  • Do not over-hedge either. Constant qualification reads as low confidence. Be decisive where you know, honest where you do not.
  • "I don't know, but here's how I'd approach finding out" is a genuinely strong answer, not a fallback.
Say this

I don't know that off the top of my head. Here's how I'd find out, and here's what I'd expect the answer to look like — [then reason out loud].

03

Questions to ask them

Core

Always have three, and make them specific enough that only that interviewer could answer them. This is scored, informally but really.

Think of it as

The questions a buyer asks reveal how carefully they have thought about the purchase.

How it actually works
  • For engineers: "What's the thing about this codebase that surprises new engineers?" "What does the on-call rotation actually look like?" "What's a decision the team made that you'd now make differently?"
  • For the hiring manager: "What does a great first six months look like?" "What's the biggest technical risk the team is carrying right now?"
  • Avoid anything a search would answer — team size, tech stack basics, whether Google is a good place to work.
  • Avoid compensation and levelling here. Those belong with the recruiter, not in a technical round.
  • Listen to the answer and follow up. A real conversation is the point; a checklist recited is not.
//The Plan: Today to Offer

The Plan: Today to Offer

Concrete, dated, and built around the constraint you cannot move — Google's pipeline runs three and a half to five months from referral, and team match is the unpredictable tail.

01

The timeline, worked backwards

On your résuméCore

For an offer in Jan–Feb 2027, the referral has to land by roughly mid-October 2026. Today is 22 August 2026, so you have about eight weeks to be interview-ready before the clock starts.

Think of it as

A flight with a fixed departure. The only variable is how prepared you are when the gate opens, and the gate does not wait.

How it actually works
  • Now → mid-Oct 2026 (8 weeks): get interview-ready *and* run the referral outreach in parallel. Do not sequence these — the referral takes weeks of its own.
  • Mid-Oct → Nov: referral lands, recruiter screen, technical screen. Peak coding sharpness needs to be here.
  • Nov → Dec: onsite loop. Four to five rounds, usually within a two-week window.
  • Dec → Feb 2027: hiring committee, then team match. Team match is the unpredictable tail and the reason Jan–Feb is realistic and December is not.
  • The pipeline is the constraint, not your preparation. Every week you delay outreach moves the offer date by a week — preparation can happen in parallel, referrals cannot be compressed.
Trap

Waiting until you feel ready before starting the referral outreach. The outreach takes 4–6 weeks on its own, and you can be preparing throughout. Starting it late is the single most common way this timeline slips a quarter.

02

The referral plan

On your résuméCore

You have no existing Google contact, so the route is LinkedIn outreach to ex-Zoho engineers now at Google India. Shared employer is the strongest cold hook available to you.

Think of it as

A warm introduction is a door held open. A cold application is a letterbox.

How it actually works
  • Target list: search LinkedIn for people whose experience includes both Zoho and Google, based in India. Aim for a list of 25–30.
  • Expect roughly 10 conversations to yield 1 referral. Volume is the plan, not persuasion.
  • The message is short and specific: shared employer, one line on what you do now, one concrete reason for the team or area, and a clear small ask.
  • Ask for a conversation, not a referral, in the first message. A referral request from a stranger is easy to decline; fifteen minutes about their team is not.
  • Make it trivially easy to refer you: attach the résumé, name the job IDs, and give them two sentences they can paste into the referral form.
  • Follow up once, after 7–10 days. Then move on — no third message.
  • Referral is not a shortcut past the bar. It gets your résumé read by a human. The loop is unchanged.
Say this

Hi — I saw you were at Zoho before Google. I'm still on the CharmHealth side, now on the AI layer in billing. I'm looking at [specific team/area] and would really value fifteen minutes on what the work is actually like there. Happy to work around your calendar.

03

The eight-week preparation split

Core

Coding is the highest-variance round and the one you can most reliably improve. Weight your time accordingly, and treat the behavioural round as real preparation rather than something you will improvise.

Think of it as

Training for a decathlon where two events carry most of the points. You still turn up for the rest.

How it actually works
  • ~50% coding. Consistent daily volume in Python. Use the DSA Lab's 30-day program as the spine, and prioritise patterns over problem count.
  • ~20% system design. Rehearse the five worked designs in the System Design track out loud, timed to 45 minutes, on a whiteboard or blank page.
  • ~15% résumé depth. Every module in the Résumé track drilled until each number and mechanism is instant.
  • ~15% behavioural. Eight stories, rehearsed aloud, timed to two and a half minutes. This is the most under-invested and cheapest-to-improve round.
  • Mock interviews are non-negotiable. At least four, with a real person, under time pressure. Solving problems alone does not train the performance.
  • Record yourself once. It is unpleasant and it will fix more communication problems than any amount of reading.
04

The one thing to fix on your résumé

On your résuméCore

You have business metrics everywhere and engineering scale nowhere. There is no QPS, no latency percentile, no concurrency figure, no data volume anywhere on the page. For an L4 loop that is the highest-leverage gap you can close.

Think of it as

A chef's CV listing revenue and covers but never plates per service. Throughput is what the kitchen judges you on.

How it actually works
  • Go and pull, this week: peak QPS and p50/p95 latency on the services you own; concurrent users at peak; row counts on your largest tables and total storage.
  • Specifically: Copilot requests per day through the agentic runtime, real before/after percentiles for the rebuild, e-KYC verifications per day at peak, and the billing ledger's write rate.
  • Then rewrite two bullets with the pattern: what changed + by how much + at what load + which percentile.
  • Never invent one. A real outcome without scale beats an invented QPS, and a fabricated number collapses under a single follow-up.
  • Where you genuinely cannot get it, have a bounded honest answer ready — the load shape, tenant count, and clinic-hours diurnal pattern still show you think in terms of load.
  • This is also an interview answer, not just a résumé edit. "What scale does your service run at?" is a question you must not fumble.
Trap

This is the single highest-value hour of work available to you right now, and it is easy to keep postponing because it requires pulling real dashboards rather than writing. Do it this week.

05

Three things that would strengthen the packet

Deep

Beyond preparation: what would actually change how a hiring committee reads you, in the time available.

Think of it as

Polishing versus adding a room. Some of this is presentation; one of them is genuinely new evidence.

How it actually works
  • Public evidence of the AI depth. Your strongest differentiator — an in-house agentic runtime, prompt versioning, evals — is entirely invisible outside your company. Two or three substantial technical write-ups on latency in agentic systems or evaluating RAG in a regulated domain would make it verifiable. This is the highest-leverage addition and it also sharpens how you explain the work.
  • A verifiable open-source or side artefact. Even a small, well-engineered tool with tests, CI and a real README is evidence a committee can inspect. Quality over ambition — one polished thing beats five abandoned ones.
  • Competitive programming currency. Your accomplishments are strong but dated to 2021–22. A current LeetCode contest rating is both preparation and a signal, and it costs you nothing extra because you are practising anyway.
  • What not to bother with: more certifications. They carry close to zero weight at Google and consume time that coding practice would use better.
  • One more honest note: four years at one product in one domain is your main levelling risk. Counter it by leading with breadth of *problem types* — identity, billing, ML systems, developer tooling, security — rather than breadth of employer.
06

The week before, and the day of

Core

The last week is for consolidation and sleep, not new material. Learning a new algorithm three days out costs more in confidence than it adds in coverage.

Think of it as

The night before a marathon you rest. You do not attempt a personal best.

How it actually works
  • Final week: re-solve problems you have already done, re-read this guide's trap boxes, rehearse the eight stories aloud. No new topics.
  • Day before: one light problem to stay warm, then stop. Sleep matters more than one more medium.
  • Set up properly: stable connection, backup device, water, paper for diagrams, the coding environment tested in advance.
  • First five minutes of each round: slow down deliberately. Clarify, restate, and give the brute force. The instinct under adrenaline is to rush, and rushing is what loses rounds.
  • Between rounds, reset. A bad round is one score of four or five. Candidates who carry a poor round into the next one lose two instead of one.
  • Use the drill mode in this guide the morning of — questions only, answers hidden. It is the fastest way to find what has gone soft.
Say this

Let me make sure I understand the problem before I start — [restate it]. And let me check a couple of constraints: how large can the input get, and can there be duplicates?
